questions.q: Software is described as a dominant factor of change for new products, driven by three key issues. Which of the following is one of those three key issues?
o: Cloud migration
Agile transformation
Arbitrary complexity
Waterfall adoption
questions.e: The three key issues that make software a dominant factor of change are arbitrary complexity (integrated software in most complex systems), instant distribution (rapid global distribution), and use of "off-the-shelf" bought-in ready-made components. Waterfall, Agile, and cloud migration are not among these three.

questions.q: The use of bought-in, ready-made components that reduce the product development cycle is referred to by which term?
o: Rapid prototyping
"Off-the-shelf" components
Instant distribution
Arbitrary complexity
questions.e: "Off-the-shelf" components denote bought-in and ready-made components that reduce the product development cycle. Instant distribution refers to rapid global distribution, and arbitrary complexity refers to integrated software in complex systems.

questions.q: One viewpoint defines requirements engineering as the branch of software engineering concerned with the real-world goals for, functions of, and constraints on software systems, and with the relationship of these factors to precise specifications of software behaviour and their evolution over time and across software families. This definition is attributed to whom?
o: Zave (1997)
Ebert (2010)
Royce (1975)
Sommerville (2005)
questions.e: The Software Engineering Viewpoint definition of requirements engineering, concerning real-world goals, functions, and constraints and their relationship to precise specifications and evolution across software families, is attributed to Zave (1997). Sommerville is associated with the three requirement levels, and Royce with poor management consequences.

questions.q: According to the IEEE definition (IEEE-STD-1220-1998), a requirement is a statement identifying a product or process characteristic or constraint that must be which of the following?
o: Unambiguous, testable or measurable, and necessary for acceptability
Informal, abstract, and stakeholder-approved
Aspirational, negotiable, and high-level
Formal, mathematical, and rigorous
questions.e: The IEEE definition (IEEE-STD-1220-1998) states a requirement must be unambiguous, testable or measurable, and necessary for product or process acceptability by consumers or internal quality assurance guidelines. The other options mix in traits not part of this specific definition.

questions.q: How is the distinction between a goal and a requirement characterised?
o: Goals are testable statements, while requirements are abstract objectives
Goals are derived from requirements through analysis
Goals apply to software, while requirements apply only to hardware
Goals are high-level objectives, while a requirement specifies how a goal should be accomplished by a proposed system
questions.e: Goals are high-level objectives of a business, organization, or system, whereas a requirement specifies how a goal should be accomplished by a proposed system. The relationship is not reversed, and both apply beyond a single domain.

questions.q: Sommerville (2005) suggests three levels of requirements classification. Which set correctly names these three levels?
o: User, System, Design requirements
Informal, Formal, Semiformal requirements
Business, Technical, Political requirements
Functional, Non-functional, Domain requirements
questions.e: Sommerville (2005) proposes three requirement levels: User requirements, System requirements, and Design requirements. Functional/Non-functional/Domain is a separate taxonomy based on requirement type, not Sommerville's three levels.

questions.q: Abstract statements written in natural language that specify what services the system is expected to provide and any constraints, sometimes termed a "concept of operations" (Conops), describe which requirement level?
o: User requirements
Design requirements
System requirements
Domain requirements
questions.e: User requirements are abstract natural-language statements specifying the services (user functionality) the system provides and any constraints; they are often termed a "concept of operations" (Conops) and in Agile are presented as User Stories. System requirements, by contrast, are detailed and precise.

questions.q: Detailed descriptions of services and constraints that are sometimes referred to as a functional specification and are collected in an SRS document correspond to which requirement level?
o: System requirements
Business requirements
User requirements
Design requirements
questions.e: System requirements are detailed descriptions of services and constraints, sometimes called a functional specification, derived from analysis of user requirements, structured and precise, and collected in a systems requirements specification (SRS) document. Use cases can play the role of system requirements.

questions.q: Under the taxonomy that classifies requirements by type, which of the following is one of the three listed types?
o: Design requirements
User requirements
Domain requirements
Political requirements
questions.e: The type-based taxonomy lists Functional requirements (FRs), Non-functional requirements (NFRs), and Domain requirements. User and Design requirements belong instead to Sommerville's three-level classification, and Political is a category of NFR.

questions.q: Beyond describing the services a system should provide and how it reacts to its inputs, what additional obligation is placed on functional requirements?
o: They must be limited to high-level statements only
They must exclude any mention of inputs and outputs
They must explicitly state certain behaviours that the system should not do
They must always be expressed using formal methods
questions.e: Functional requirements describe the services the system should provide and how it reacts to inputs, and in addition must explicitly state certain behaviours that the system should NOT do. They can be high-level or detailed and may use natural language, visual models, or formal methods.

questions.q: Which statement about non-functional requirements (NFRs) is accurate?
o: They receive more attention than functional requirements in practice
They help distinguish between competing functionally equivalent products and still receive little attention relative to FRs
They are imposed solely by the developers rather than the operating environment
They are objective, absolute, and confined to a single module
questions.e: NFRs are imposed by the environment in which the system operates, help distinguish between competing functionally equivalent products, are subjective, relative, and scattered among multiple modules, and still receive little attention relative to FRs. They are therefore not objective, absolute, or single-module confined.

questions.q: The observation that enhancing software security may come at the expense of performance (for example by increasing latency) illustrates which property of non-functional requirements?
o: That NFRs receive more attention than functional requirements
That NFRs are easy to trace and estimate
That achieving one NFR can help or hinder the achievement of other NFRs
That NFRs are always independent of one another
questions.e: NFRs can interact so that achieving one can help or hinder others; the security-versus-performance (latency) example shows this trade-off. These interactions create a network of interdependencies and trade-offs that is not easy to trace or estimate.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the categories of non-functional requirements?
o: Political/Cultural
User
Domain
Behavioural
questions.e: The five categories of NFRs are Quality, Design, Economic, Operating, and Political/Cultural. Domain and User relate to other classifications, and Behavioural is not one of the listed categories.

questions.q: Safety, Privacy, Reliability, Usability, and Maintainability are cited as typical examples of which kind of requirement?
o: Quality requirements
Design requirements
Domain requirements
Functional requirements
questions.e: Safety, Privacy, Reliability, Usability, and Maintainability are given as typical quality requirements. Quality is defined (ISO12601) as the totality of characteristics of an entity that bear on its ability to satisfy stated and implied needs; generally any attribute ending in "ility" is a non-functional requirement.

questions.q: A quality taxonomy covering 87 qualities, decomposing quality into structured characteristics and sub-characteristics, is attributed to whom?
o: Neto et al. (2000)
Zave (1997)
Kassab (2009)
Ebert (2010)
questions.e: Kassab (2009) presented a quality taxonomy for 87 qualities. Neto et al. (2000) enumerated problems arising from NFR omission, and Zave (1997) provided the software-engineering definition of RE.

questions.q: In 1992 a new computer-aided dispatch system was introduced that became extremely inefficient, failed completely, and forced a reversion to the previous manual system. Which organisation experienced this failure, mainly attributed to a failure to consider human and organizational factors?
o: National Library of Medicine MEDLARS II
NASA Mars Climate Orbiter
New Jersey Department of Motor Vehicles
The London Ambulance Service (LAS)
questions.e: The London Ambulance Service (LAS) introduced a computer-aided dispatch system in 1992 that failed completely, forcing reversion to the manual system; the failure was mainly due to not considering human and organizational factors (Finkelstein and Dowell, 1996).

questions.q: The NASA Mars Climate Orbiter was destroyed because ground software worked in pounds force while the spacecraft expected Newtons, causing the thrusters' effect to be underestimated. By what factor was the effect underestimated?
questions.e: The Mars Climate Orbiter failure involved a metric/English units mix-up: the thrusters' effect was underestimated by a factor of 4.45, the ratio between a pound force and a Newton (Breitman et al. 1999).

questions.q: The New Jersey Department of Motor Vehicles licensing system was written in a fourth generation programming language to save development time but ran so slowly that many vehicles had unprocessed renewals. Which problem is cited as the cause of this failure?
o: Software interoperability
Portability and evolvability problems
Human and organizational factors
Performance scalability problems
questions.e: The New Jersey DMV licensing system aimed at affordability and timeliness objectives but failed due to performance scalability problems (Babcock 1985). Interoperability caused the Mars Orbiter failure; portability/evolvability relate to the MEDLARS II case.

questions.q: The National Library of Medicine MEDLARS II system was built with many layers of abstraction focused on improving portability and evolvability, yet was scrapped after two expensive hardware upgrades. What problem caused it to be scrapped?
o: Incomplete requirements
Human and organizational factors
Interoperability problems
Performance problems
questions.e: The MEDLARS II system initially focused on portability and evolvability qualities but was scrapped after two expensive hardware upgrades due to performance problems (Boehm and In, 1996).

questions.q: In the Standish Group surveys of 1995 and 1996, which reason was identified as the single largest contributor to project failure?
o: Lack of user involvement (12.4%)
Incomplete requirements (13.1%)
Lack of resources (10.6%)
Unrealistic expectations (9.9%)
questions.e: In the Standish Group 1995 and 1996 surveys, incomplete requirements topped the list of failure reasons at 13.1%, followed by lack of user involvement at 12.4% and lack of resources at 10.6%.

questions.q: In the traditional-view analysis of the Standish Group success factors, which factor ranked highest as a contributor to project success?
o: Clear statement of requirements (13.0%)
User involvement (15.9%)
Proper planning (9.6%)
Management support (13.9%)
questions.e: The listed project success factors rank user involvement highest at 15.9%, followed by management support at 13.9% and clear statement of requirements at 13.0% (Standish Group 1995 & 1996).

questions.q: The traditional-view project-failure problems are grouped into three main categories. Which of the following is one of those three categories?
o: Politics
Documentation
Deployment
Testing
questions.e: The three main categories of failure problems are Requirements, Management problems of resources, and Politics (which contributes to the first two). Testing, deployment, and documentation are not among these three categories.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the five requirements engineering activities?
o: Requirements compilation
Requirements elicitation/discovery
Requirements auditing
Requirements deployment
questions.e: The five RE activities are requirements elicitation/discovery, analysis and reconciliation, representation/modelling, verification and validation, and management. Deployment, compilation, and auditing are not among the listed activities.

questions.q: The requirements engineering process begins with a phase in which basic questions are asked and the reasons, objectives, and feasibility of the project are established. What is this phase called?
o: Reconciliation
Verification
Elicitation
Inception
questions.e: The RE process starts with inception, in which all the basic questions are asked and the reasons, objectives, and feasibility of the project are established. Elicitation, reconciliation, and verification are later activities.

questions.q: Brainstorming, interviews, task observations, use cases/scenarios, and prototyping are presented as techniques for which RE activity?
o: Requirements elicitation/discovery
Requirements management
Requirements verification and validation
Requirements representation/modelling
questions.e: Brainstorming, interviews, task observations, use cases/scenarios, and prototyping are listed as techniques for requirements elicitation/discovery, which involves uncovering what the customer needs and wants.

questions.q: Requirements representation techniques are grouped into three kinds. A representation described as convertible to a sound representation, or able to be made fully formal by adding a semantic framework, is termed which of the following?
o: Formal
Abstract
Informal
Semiformal
questions.e: Requirements representation techniques are informal (natural language, sketches, diagrams), formal (mathematically sound), and semiformal (convertible to a sound representation, or made fully formal by adding a semantic framework). The described case is semiformal.

questions.q: Within requirements verification and validation, which activity is associated with the question "Am I building the right product?" and refers back to the stakeholders?
o: Requirements management
Requirements elicitation
Requirements verification
Requirements validation
questions.e: Requirements validation determines whether the specification is a correct representation of customer needs, checking that the right product is being built (referring back to stakeholders): "Am I building the right product?" Verification instead checks that the product is being built right.

questions.q: Requirements verification checks that the product is being built correctly. During the requirements engineering phase itself, what does verification mainly involve?
o: Checking consistency between different requirements and detecting conflicts
Managing scope creep and traceability
Referring back to stakeholders to confirm needs
Deriving software requirements from system requirements
questions.e: Requirements verification checks that the product is being built right; during RE it mainly involves checking consistency between different requirements and detecting conflicts, whereas during design it refers back to the specification. Referring to stakeholders is validation.

questions.q: Requirements management involves coping with changing requirements over time. Which of the following is identified as a cause of requirements change?
o: Domain vocabulary differences
Formal review techniques
Better understanding of the problem
Use of off-the-shelf components
questions.e: Requirements management copes with changes caused by business process changes, technology changes, and better understanding of the problem, and stresses traceability. Formal review is a V&V technique, not a cause of change.

questions.q: In requirements management, what term describes the situation that managers must learn to intelligently push back against?
o: Scope creep
Feature freeze
Requirements traceability
Change control
questions.e: Requirements management notes that managers need the skills to intelligently push back when scope creep ensues, and that traceability and change-tracking tools ease the management burden.

questions.q: Ebert (2010) suggests that requirements engineers should have competency in a set of areas. Which of the following is one of those competency areas?
o: Finance
Cognition
Procurement
Marketing
questions.e: Ebert (2010) lists competency areas as requirements engineering, systems engineering, management, communication, cognition, and social interaction. Marketing, finance, and procurement are not among these areas.

questions.q: Which characterisation of the requirements engineer's role is emphasised, notably by Karl Wiegers?
o: RE is purely a technical modelling exercise
RE requires no communication with users
RE is solely the responsibility of developers
RE is more than just modelling and is a social activity
questions.e: The requirements engineer plays an essential communication role, translating user requirements into functional requirements and quality goals; Karl Wiegers emphasises that RE is more than just modelling, it is a social activity.

questions.q: Two extremes of requirements documents are contrasted. An informal outline of the requirements using a few paragraphs or simple diagrams is called which of the following?
o: Requirements Specification
Requirements Definition
Elicitation notes
Vision and Scope Document
questions.e: The two extremes are the Requirements Definition (an informal outline using a few paragraphs or simple diagrams) and the Requirements Specification (a long list of tens or hundreds of pages of intricate requirements). The described informal outline is the Requirements Definition.

questions.q: When undertaking the development of a new system or the redesign of an old one, what is described as the first thing that needs to be obtained or developed?
o: A complete list of all stakeholders
A prioritized ranking of requirements
A concise description of what the system is supposed to do
A context diagram of the system boundaries
questions.e: The first step in developing a new system or redesigning an old one is to obtain or develop a concise description of what it is supposed to do. This concise description is what becomes the product mission statement.

questions.q: A concise description of what a system is supposed to do is most commonly called which of the following?
o: A product (or system) mission statement
A context diagram
A rich picture
A CRACK statement
questions.e: A concise description of what a system is supposed to do is often called a product mission statement (or system mission statement). Some organizations instead call it a concept of operations (Conops) statement, and in agile it is termed a system metaphor.

questions.q: An elaborated, high-level requirements specification document that some organizations use in place of a product mission statement is referred to by which term?
o: Rich picture
Concept of operations (Conops) statement
Context diagram
System metaphor
questions.e: Some organizations refer to the mission statement as a concept of operations (Conops) statement, which can be a very elaborated document amounting to a high-level requirements specification. The term 'system metaphor' is instead used in the agile approach.

questions.q: In agile approaches, a product mission statement is often referred to by which term?
o: Concept of operations
System metaphor
Rich picture
Gadfly
questions.e: In the agile approach, the product mission statement is often termed the 'system metaphor.' A concept of operations (Conops) statement is a different, more elaborate alternative used by some organizations.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the guidance given about how a requirements engineer should treat what customers ask for?
o: Always assume you know what the customer really wants and build it
Customers always know exactly what they want and can state it clearly
Providing customers with more than they have asked for is not helpful
Providing extra features beyond the request is always beneficial
questions.e: Among the lessons about encounters with customers, providing customers with more than they have asked for is not helpful. Related points warn never to make assumptions and note that customers do not always know what they want and can communicate poorly even when they do.

questions.q: What is described as a necessary first step in identifying stakeholders?
o: Prioritizing the stakeholders by importance
Writing a full requirements specification
Conducting intensive group meetings
Creating a high-level systems model that defines the system boundary
questions.e: A necessary first step in identifying stakeholders is to create a high-level systems model, which identifies the people and entities involved and defines the system boundary. Without correctly defining boundaries, important stakeholders may be overlooked.

questions.q: A visual diagram for a system of interest that shows system boundaries and interactions with other systems, people, and the environment is called what?
o: A mission statement
A context diagram
A Maslow hierarchy
A rich picture
questions.e: A context diagram is a visual representation for a system of interest showing system boundaries and interactions with other systems, people, and the environment. A use case or block diagram can be used for this purpose.

questions.q: A context diagram is described as important for how many reasons?
o: Five
Three
Two
Four
questions.e: The context diagram is important for three reasons: it provides a basis for dialog, helps in combating scope creep, and helps in requirements agreement and analysis when discussing ambiguous, complex, and missing requirements.

questions.q: The unchecked growth of functional requirements beyond the intent of the system is defined as which of the following?
o: Desiderata
Requirements prioritization
Scope creep
Power distance
questions.e: Scope creep is defined as the unchecked growth of functional requirements beyond the intent of the system. Combating scope creep is cited as one of the three reasons a context diagram is important.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a stakeholder?
o: Government agencies that regulate aspects of the system
The set of individuals who have some interest (a stake) in the success or failure of the system in question
Only the engineers responsible for building and testing the system
Anyone who pays for the system regardless of interest
questions.e: Stakeholders represent the set of individuals who have some interest (a stake) in the success or failure of the system in question. Customers, sponsors, regulators, and society are among the listed types, but the definition is broader than any single type.

questions.q: Individuals who may be adversely affected by a system, such as competitors, investors, and people whose jobs will be displaced, are referred to as which type of stakeholder?
o: CRACK stakeholders
Gadflies
Sponsors
Negative stakeholders
questions.e: Negative stakeholders are those who may be adversely affected by the system, including competitors, investors, and people whose jobs will be changed, adversely affected, or displaced. The guidance stresses not ignoring negative stakeholders.

questions.q: The term 'gadflies' is used to describe which group of people?
o: Individuals not directly affected by a system who are nonetheless interested in or opposed to it and wield power or influence
The engineers responsible for maintenance and testing
Sponsors who have commissioned and will pay for the system
Customers who repeatedly change their minds about requirements
questions.e: 'Gadflies' are individuals not directly affected by systems who are interested in or opposed to them and, because they may wield power or influence, must be considered. Examples include environmentalists, animal activists, single-issue zealots, and advocates.

questions.q: Boehm coined the acronym CRACK to assist stakeholder identification. What does the 'A' in CRACK stand for?
o: Accountable for the budget
Authorized to make decisions
Adversely affected
Available at all times
questions.e: In Boehm's CRACK acronym a good stakeholder is Committed, Represents a group of stakeholders, Authorized to make decisions, will Collaborate with team members, and is Knowledgeable. The 'A' stands for Authorized to make decisions.

questions.q: In Boehm's CRACK characterization of a good stakeholder, what does the letter 'C' at the start of the acronym stand for?
o: Critical of requirements
Committed to the project
Certified by management
Cautious about scope
questions.e: In CRACK, the leading 'C' stands for Committed to the project. The remaining letters denote Represents a group, Authorized to make decisions, will Collaborate with team members, and is Knowledgeable.

questions.q: A cartoon-like, informal drawing that shows various users along with their goals, wants, and needs, and that can aid stakeholder identification, is known as what?
o: A rich picture
A use-case block diagram
A context diagram
A Conops statement
questions.e: A rich picture is a cartoon-like drawing, a feature of Soft Systems Methodology (SSM), that shows various users along with their goals, wants, and needs. Rich pictures resemble annotated use-case diagrams or concept maps but are rather informal.

questions.q: Which system-based approach is recommended for identifying the complete set of stakeholders when developing novel systems?
o: Maslow's hierarchy
Concept of operations
Soft Systems Methodology (SSM)
CRACK analysis
questions.e: Because identifying a complete set of stakeholders is difficult for novel systems, a system-based approach like Soft Systems Methodology (SSM) can be used. SSM features the rich picture as a tool useful in stakeholder identification.

questions.q: What is described as the primary goal of the requirements engineer with respect to the customer?
o: To understand what the customer wants or desires (desiderata)
To define the system boundaries
To write the product mission statement
To rank stakeholders by importance
questions.e: The primary goal of the requirements engineer is to understand what the customer wants or desires, referred to as desiderata. Requirement prioritization is offered as a way to reconcile these wants and needs.

questions.q: Customers' wants and needs are said to exist at various levels. Which of the following is one of the levels described?
o: Financial (it must maximize return on investment)
Competitive (it should be better than brand X)
Environmental (it must be safe for physical systems)
Regulatory (it must satisfy government agencies)
questions.e: Customer wants and needs are described at levels including practical (minimum functionality), competitive (it should be better than brand X), and selfish (wanting to show off the system's features). Competitive is one such level.

questions.q: According to Maslow's theory as applied to customer needs, what happens if lower levels of needs are not satisfied first?
o: People will never move very far up the pyramid or stay at a higher level
The customer changes their mind about requirements
The higher-level needs become impossible to define
The system automatically prioritizes those needs
questions.e: Maslow's theory holds that humans satisfy needs starting with the most basic and work upward, but they will never move very far up the pyramid, or stay at a higher level, if lower levels of needs are not satisfied first.

questions.q: Which of the following is identified as a reason why customers change their minds during a project?
o: The requirements engineer refuses to negotiate
Stakeholders were divided into too many classes
The context diagram was drawn incorrectly
A change in the environment in which the system functions, such as economic or regulatory changes
questions.e: Reasons customers change their minds include that they can't see every possible requirement, requirements may change over the life cycle, and changes in the environment (physical, economic, or regulatory changes, or competition). Fickleness, ignorance, late ROI discovery, and deliberately withholding information are also listed.

questions.q: Why is prioritization or ranking of stakeholders considered useful?
o: It reduces the number of stakeholders that must be consulted
It replaces the need for a context diagram
It guarantees that all stakeholders are treated equally
It helps resolve conflicting needs and denotes the severity of risks if those needs are not met
questions.e: Because not all stakeholders are of equal importance, prioritization or ranking helps resolve conflicting needs and desires, and the ranking denotes the severity of risks if those stakeholders' needs and desires are not met.

questions.q: Among the methods of communicating with customers, which is characterized as spontaneous and informal but persistent?
o: Teleconference/video conference
In-person meetings
Written periodic status reports
Emails
questions.e: Emails are characterized as spontaneous and informal, but persistent. By contrast, in-person meetings are expensive and time consuming, written communication is impersonal and may slow communication, and teleconferencing suffers from unstable connectivity and misunderstanding.

questions.q: Which communication method is described as serving as a shared whiteboard?
o: Wiki technology
Periodic status report
Email
Teleconference
questions.e: Wiki technology is described as serving as a shared whiteboard for communicating with customers and other stakeholders. In-person meetings, group meetings, status reports, and emails are the other listed methods.

questions.q: Which piece of advice is given for managing customer expectations?
o: Set customers' expectations low deliberately and then exceed them
Over commit early to build customer confidence
Don't set customers' expectations low deliberately and then exceed them, and don't over commit
Avoid negotiating until the end of the project
questions.e: For managing expectations, the guidance is to not deliberately set customers' expectations low and then exceed them, and to not over commit. Both are cited as pitfalls to avoid.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the rules given for stakeholder negotiations?
o: Look for early successes by getting agreement on small things first to build positive momentum
Refuse to give any ground so as not to appear weak
Conclude negotiating as soon as one party is satisfied
Delay all agreements until every requirement is finalized
questions.e: Negotiation rules include looking for early successes by getting agreement on small things first to build positive momentum. Others are setting ground rules up front, understanding expectations, giving and pushing back a little, and concluding only when all parties are satisfied.

questions.q: According to the negotiation guidance, when should negotiating be concluded?
o: When the requirements engineer decides costs are too high
After the first early success is achieved
As soon as the customer agrees to the budget
Only when all parties are satisfied
questions.e: One of the negotiation rules is to conclude negotiating only when all parties are satisfied. This complements setting ground rules up front, understanding expectations, seeking early successes, and being willing to give and push back a little.

questions.q: Which cultural characteristic is described using the phrase 'power distance'?
o: Long-term orientation
Comfort in dealing with authority
Uncertainty avoidance
Tendency toward a masculine world view
questions.e: Among cultural characteristics that matter to the requirements engineer, comfort in dealing with authority is labeled 'power distance.' Other listed characteristics include individualism, the masculinity index, uncertainty avoidance, and long-term orientation.

questions.q: In requirements engineering, what best describes the problem domain?
o: The space in which a concrete solution to the user's need is defined and built
The set of software requirements imposed on a system to deliver promised features
The border between the solution and the real world surrounding it
The home of real users and other stakeholders whose needs arise from business or technical problems requiring a software solution
questions.e: The problem domain is described as the home of real users and other stakeholders, people whose needs must be addressed arising from business or technical problems for which they need a software solution. Defining a solution belongs to the solution domain, and the border between solution and real world is the system boundary.

questions.q: In the solution space, how is a 'feature of the system' defined?
o: Anyone who could be materially affected by implementation of the system
A specific requirement imposed on the solution to deliver a capability
A restriction on the degree of freedom available in providing a solution
A service provided by the system that fulfills one or more stakeholder needs
questions.e: A feature is defined as a service provided by the system that fulfills one or more stakeholder needs. A restriction on freedom is a constraint, and a specific requirement imposed to deliver features is a software requirement.

questions.q: During which phase of software development is the team focused on understanding the business case, the scope of the project, and the feasibility of an implementation?
o: Construction phase
Transition phase
Elaboration phase
Inception phase
questions.e: The inception phase is when the team focuses on understanding the business case for the project, the scope of the project, and the feasibility of an implementation.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the activities associated with the inception phase?
o: Problem analysis
Establishment of solution vision
Identification of project risk factors
Detailed coding of system modules
questions.e: The inception phase activities are problem analysis, establishment of solution vision, schedule and budget estimates, and identification of project risk factors. Detailed coding is not part of this phase, which centers on the business case, scope, and feasibility.

questions.q: What are the two outputs that problem analysis results in?
o: Context diagram and Pareto chart
Software requirements specification and test plan
Schedule estimates and budget estimates
Product Vision and Project Scope
questions.e: The goal of problem analysis is to better understand the problem before development begins, and it results in the Product Vision and Project Scope. It uses business requirements obtained from stakeholders as input.

questions.q: Leffingwell and Widrig propose five steps for problem analysis. Which of the following is the correct ordering?
o: Identify stakeholders; gain agreement on the problem; understand root causes; identify constraints; define vision and boundary
Gain agreement on the problem definition; understand the root causes; identify the stakeholders; define the solution system vision and boundary; identify the constraints
Understand root causes; gain agreement on the problem; identify stakeholders; define vision and boundary; identify constraints
Gain agreement on the problem definition; identify the stakeholders; understand root causes; identify constraints; define vision and boundary
questions.e: The five steps in order are: gain agreement on the problem definition, understand the root causes, identify the stakeholders, define the solution system vision and boundary, and identify the constraints to be imposed on the solution.

questions.q: One of the simplest ways to gain agreement on a problem is to ask stakeholders to write a problem statement in an agreed format. Which set of elements is used for this problem statement format?
o: The Problem, Stakeholders, Constraints, Solution
For, What, The, Is, That, Unlike, Our product
The Problem, Affects, Results, Benefits
Economics, Political, Technical, System
questions.e: The problem statement format uses four elements: The Problem (describe the problem), Affects (identify stakeholders affected), Results (describe the impact on stakeholders and business activity), and Benefits (indicate the proposed solution and list a few benefits). The For/What/The/Is/That/Unlike structure is the Moore vision statement template.

questions.q: In the problem statement format, what does the 'Results' element describe?
o: A description of the problem itself
The impact of the problem on stakeholders and business activity
The proposed solution and a few of its benefits
The stakeholders affected by the problem
questions.e: In the problem statement format, 'Results' describes the impact of this problem on stakeholders and business activity. 'Affects' identifies the stakeholders, 'Benefits' indicates the proposed solution and benefits, and 'The Problem' describes the problem.

questions.q: What is the purpose of root cause analysis in problem analysis?
o: To draw the boundary between what is in and out of scope
To estimate schedule and budget for the project
To find underlying causes that may not be immediately apparent behind a problem
To rank stakeholders by their attitude toward the product
questions.e: Root cause analysis consists of finding underlying causes that may not be immediately apparent, because there is often a problem (reason) behind the problem. It recursively determines contributing factors until causes are understood.

questions.q: Which tool is suggested for estimating the relative impact of root causes so that the most worthwhile ones can be addressed?
o: A Pareto (bar) chart
A context diagram
A vision statement template
A stakeholder profile table
questions.e: Because root causes do not all have the same impact and some may not be worth fixing now, the relative impact of root causes can be estimated with the help of a Pareto (bar) chart. A problem statement is then created for any root cause worth solving with an IT solution.

questions.q: Which statement best defines a stakeholder in the context of a new system?
o: Individuals, groups, or organizations actively involved in the project, affected by its outcome, or able to influence its outcome
Someone or something outside the system that interacts with it
The market opportunity that justifies building the product
Only the economic buyer who pays for the system
questions.e: Stakeholders are defined as individuals, groups, or organizations who are actively involved in the project, are affected by its outcome, or are able to influence its outcome. An external interacting entity is an actor, not the general definition of a stakeholder.

questions.q: A stakeholder profile should include several items. Which of the following is one of them?
o: The exact salary of the stakeholder
The number of releases the product will have
The major value or benefit the stakeholder will receive from the product
The programming language the stakeholder prefers
questions.e: A stakeholder profile should include the major value or benefit the stakeholder will receive (e.g., improved productivity, reduced rework, cost saving), their likely attitude toward the product, major features and characteristics of interest, and any known constraints that must be accommodated.

questions.q: How is the Product Vision distinguished from the Project Scope?
o: Both describe only the current release with identical content
The Product Vision lists constraints, while the Project Scope lists root causes
The Product Vision draws the boundary between in and out, while the Project Scope aligns stakeholders in a common direction
The Product Vision describes what the product is about and could eventually become, while the Project Scope identifies what portion of that long-term vision the current project addresses
questions.e: The Product Vision describes what the product is about and what it could eventually become, aligning all stakeholders in a common direction. The Project Scope identifies what portion of the ultimate long-term product vision the current project will address, drawing the boundary between what is in and what is out.

questions.q: The vision statement template attributed to Moore includes a clause beginning 'Unlike ...'. What does this clause capture?
o: The key benefit or compelling reason to use the product
The target customer for the product
The product category the product belongs to
The primary competitive alternative, current system, or current business process
questions.e: In Moore's vision statement template, the 'Unlike' clause identifies the primary competitive alternative, current system, or current business process, and is followed by 'Our product' stating the primary differentiation and advantages of the new product.

questions.q: What does the system boundary define?
o: The set of business risks associated with the product
The border between the solution and the real world that surrounds the solution
The list of major features planned for the initial release
The relative impact of each root cause of a problem
questions.e: The system boundary defines the border between the solution and the real world that surrounds it. Information in the form of I/O passes back and forth between the system and the users/actors living outside it, and all interactions occur via interfaces between the system and the external world.

questions.q: When defining the solution system boundary, the world is divided into 'our system' and actors. What is an actor?
o: A quantitative and measurable business benefit the product provides
A numbered list of major features unique to the new product
Someone or something, outside the system, that interacts with the system
A restriction on the degree of freedom in providing a solution
questions.e: When defining the solution system boundary, the world is divided into our system and things that interact with it, called actors. An actor is someone or something, outside the system, that interacts with the system.

questions.q: According to the treatment of scope during development, how should out-of-scope requirements that arise be handled?
o: Deferred to a following release
Rejected and permanently discarded without record
Used to redefine the system boundary automatically
Incorporated immediately regardless of priority
questions.e: Out-of-scope requirements should be deferred to a following release. New in-scope requirements may be incorporated if they are high priority relative to the baseline, which usually implies deferring or canceling other requirements or negotiating a new schedule.

questions.q: A context diagram is described as a top-level view of a system. What does it primarily show?
o: The system's boundaries and scope, identifying terminators outside the system
The Pareto ranking of root causes
The stakeholder profiles and their attitudes
The internal data structures and algorithms of the system
questions.e: A context diagram is a top-level view of a system that shows the system's boundaries and scope. It identifies terminators outside the system and shows data, control, and material flow between the terminators and the system.

questions.q: How is a constraint defined in the context of providing a solution?
o: A service provided by the system that fulfills a stakeholder need
A description of the market opportunity for the product
A restriction on the degree of freedom we have in providing a solution
A person outside the system who interacts with it
questions.e: A constraint is a restriction on the degree of freedom we have in providing a solution. Each constraint must be carefully considered because it may cause the team to reconsider its approach; sources include schedule, ROI, budget, environment, OS, DB, and company policies.

questions.q: In the classification of potential system constraints, which source has 'internal or external political issues' and 'inter-departmental problems' as sample considerations?
o: Political
Economics
System
Technical
questions.e: Under the Political source of constraints, the sample considerations are internal or external political issues and inter-departmental problems. Economics covers financial/budget and costs of goods; Technical covers restrictions in choice of technology; System covers existing systems and compatibility.

questions.q: Within the Vision and Scope Document, the 'Limitations' portion of scope and limitations is meant to record what?
o: The business opportunity and market need
Capabilities the product won't include and rejected requirements with the reason for rejecting them
The relative impact of each root cause
The numbered list of major features unique to the new product
questions.e: The Limitations part of scope and limitations records capabilities that the product won't include (what the system is not) and rejected requirements along with the reason for rejecting them. Major features and business opportunity are documented in separate parts of the document.

questions.q: Which of the following is described as a major content item of the 'Vision of the solution' section within the Vision and Scope Document?
o: Project priorities agreed by stakeholders
Major features as a numbered list of major features or user capabilities unique to the new product
The operating environment for the system
The context diagram of terminators
questions.e: The Vision of the solution section includes the vision statement, major features (a numbered list of major features or user capabilities unique to the new product), assumptions made while developing vision and scope, and major dependencies on external factors. Project priorities and operating environment appear in a later part of the document.

questions.q: Under the business requirements, 'Business Objectives and Success Criteria' are meant to state important business benefits in what way?
o: In a quantitative and measurable way
As a top-level context diagram
As a numbered list of actors
As rejected requirements with reasons
questions.e: Business objectives and success criteria state the important business benefits the product will provide in a quantitative and measurable way, such as capturing a major market share or achieving positive cash flow within a short time period.

questions.q: How is a functional requirement best defined?
o: A high-level business objective of the organization that builds a product
A policy, guideline, standard, or regulation that constrains some aspect of the business
A description of a behavior that a system will exhibit under specific conditions
A property or characteristic that a system must exhibit or a constraint it must respect
questions.e: A functional requirement describes a behavior a system will exhibit under specific conditions. A property or characteristic the system must exhibit instead defines a nonfunctional requirement, a high-level organizational aim defines a business requirement, and a policy, guideline, standard or regulation defines a business rule.

questions.q: Which statement correctly defines a nonfunctional requirement?
o: A top-level requirement for a product containing multiple subsystems
A description of a property or characteristic that a system must exhibit, or a constraint it must respect
A behavior the system exhibits under specific conditions
A goal or task specific user classes must be able to perform
questions.e: A nonfunctional requirement describes a property or characteristic that a system must exhibit or a constraint it must respect. Behaviors under specific conditions are functional requirements, tasks users perform are user requirements, and top-level multi-subsystem requirements are system requirements.

questions.q: A quality attribute is best characterized as which of the following?
o: A kind of nonfunctional requirement that describes a service or performance characteristic of a product
A restriction imposed on the developer's design choices
A kind of functional requirement written as a 'shall' statement
A high-level business objective of the organization
questions.e: A quality attribute is a kind of nonfunctional requirement that describes a service or performance characteristic of a product, such as performance, safety, availability, or portability.

questions.q: What is the primary focus of business requirements?
o: The goals or tasks users must be able to perform with the product
The detailed services of the system useful for design and development
Why the organization is implementing the system and the business benefits it hopes to achieve
The behaviors the developers must implement under specific conditions
questions.e: Business requirements describe why the organization is implementing the system and the business benefits (financial, efficiency, market share) it hopes to achieve, focusing on the business objectives of the organization or customer. Detailed services relate to system requirements, user tasks to user requirements, and behaviors to functional requirements.

questions.q: In which document are business requirements often recorded?
o: A vision and scope document
An event-response table
A use-case model
A software requirements specification (SRS)
questions.e: Business requirements are often recorded in a vision and scope document. Other strategic guiding documents include a project charter, business case, and market requirements document. The SRS instead documents functional requirements.

questions.q: Which of the following is a way to represent user requirements?
o: Use cases, user stories, and event-response tables
Business case and project charter
Software requirements specification
Vision and scope document
questions.e: User requirements can be represented using use cases, user stories, and event-response tables. The SRS documents functional requirements, while the vision and scope document, business case, and project charter capture business requirements.

questions.q: The statement 'As a passenger, I want to check in for a flight so I can board my airplane' is an example of which representation?
o: A business rule
A user story
A design constraint
A functional 'shall' statement
questions.e: This phrasing is a user story, one of the ways to represent user requirements. The same requirement expressed as a use case would be 'Check in for a flight.' A functional requirement, by contrast, is typically written as a 'shall' statement.

questions.q: Functional requirements are often written in which traditional form?
o: Vision-and-scope narratives
'As a [role], I want...' user-story form
Property-and-measure tables
'Shall' statements
questions.e: Functional requirements are often written as traditional 'shall' statements, for example 'The Passenger shall be able to print boarding passes for all flight segments for which he has checked in.' The 'As a [role]' form is a user story.

questions.q: Who documents functional requirements in a software requirements specification (SRS)?
o: The marketing department
The product visionary
The business analyst, also referred to as the requirements analyst
The funding sponsor
questions.e: The business analyst (BA), also referred to as the requirements analyst, documents functional requirements in a software requirements specification (SRS) that describes the expected behavior of the software system. Sponsors, visionaries, and marketing are stakeholders who generate business requirements.

questions.q: In the context of system requirements, what does the term 'system' refer to?
o: A single reusable software module
A product composed of multiple components or subsystems, which can be all software or both software and hardware
Only an information system built entirely in software
Only the hardware devices interacting under software control
questions.e: A system in this sense is a product composed of multiple components or subsystems; it can be all software or include both software and hardware, and people and processes are part of a system too. It is explicitly not just any information system.

questions.q: Which example is used to illustrate a 'system' composed of interacting hardware devices under software control?
o: An airline check-in kiosk
A cashier's workstation in a supermarket
An anti-malware product
A library management system
questions.e: The cashier's workstation in a supermarket is given as a good example of a system: a bar code scanner integrated with a scale, a hand-held scanner, keyboard, display, cash drawer, card reader, PIN pad, and up to three printers, all interacting under software control.

questions.q: Why are business rules not themselves considered software requirements?
o: They are always too vague to implement
They are documented in the SRS rather than a vision document
They apply only to hardware components
They have an existence beyond the boundaries of any specific software application
questions.e: Business rules (corporate policies, government regulations, industry standards, computational algorithms) are not themselves software requirements because they exist beyond the boundaries of any specific software application, though they often dictate that the system must contain functionality to comply with them.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as an example of a business rule?
o: Performance, safety, availability, and portability
Corporate policies, government regulations, industry standards, and computational algorithms
Use cases and user stories
Inputs, outputs, stored data, and computations
questions.e: Business rules include corporate policies, government regulations, industry standards, and computational algorithms. Performance and portability are quality attributes, while inputs, outputs, and computations are concerns of functional requirements.

questions.q: A feature is defined as which of the following?
o: A goal or task a user must be able to perform with a system
A top-level requirement for a multi-subsystem product
One or more logically related system capabilities that provide value to a user and are described by a set of functional requirements
A restriction imposed on the developer's design choices
questions.e: A feature consists of one or more logically related system capabilities that provide value to a user and are described by a set of functional requirements. A feature can encompass multiple user requirements and can be hierarchically decomposed into smaller features.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as an example of a feature?
o: Web browser bookmarks and automatic virus signature updating
The cashier's workstation
A vision and scope document
A boarding pass 'shall' statement
questions.e: Examples of features include web browser bookmarks, spelling checkers, the ability to define a custom workout program on exercise equipment, and automatic virus signature updating in an anti-malware product.

questions.q: When comparing user requirements and system requirements by abstraction, which statement is accurate?
o: Both are written only in structured tables
User requirements are at a higher abstraction level, written in natural language readable by everybody, while system requirements are more detailed and precise
User requirements are more detailed and precise than system requirements
System requirements are the first attempt at describing requirements
questions.e: User requirements sit at a higher abstraction level, are usually the first attempt at describing requirements, are written in natural language or diagrams, and are readable by everybody. System requirements are lower-level: detailed, precise, cover all cases, and use a structured presentation.

questions.q: In the library example, the requirement 'The library system should provide a way to allow a user to borrow a book from the library' is an example of what?
o: A business rule
A user requirement
A design constraint
A system requirement
questions.e: This high-level statement is a user requirement. The corresponding system requirement adds detail, specifying withdrawal by ISBN and copy number and listing failure conditions such as the book already being withdrawn or the user having already withdrawn 5 books.

questions.q: In the detailed library system requirement, a withdrawal interaction fails if the user has already withdrawn how many books?
o: 20 books
5 books
3 books
10 books
questions.e: The system requirement states the withdrawal interaction fails if the user has already withdrawn 5 books (along with other conditions such as the book being already withdrawn, not in the collection, or on hold by someone else).

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the concerns addressed by functional requirements?
o: The cost and delivery date of the project
The mean time to failure and probability of unavailability
What inputs the system should accept and what outputs it should produce
The programming language and database technology to be used
questions.e: Functional requirements address what inputs the system should accept, what outputs it should produce, what data it should store, what computations it should perform, and the timing and synchronization of these. Mean time to failure is a reliability measure, and cost/delivery date and technology choices are nonfunctional constraints.

questions.q: By what other names are non-functional requirements sometimes called?
o: Quality requirements, quality of service, or extra-functional requirements
Business rules or domain requirements
System requirements or user requirements
Shall statements or use cases
questions.e: Non-functional requirements are sometimes called quality requirements, quality of service, or extra-functional requirements. They are important because if they are not met the system is useless, and they may be difficult to state precisely and to verify.

questions.q: Which set correctly names the three main categories of non-functional requirements?
o: System/Product Quality requirements, Design constraints (Process Requirements), and Commercial constraints
Business, user, and system requirements
Speed, size, and reliability requirements
Functional, domain, and emergent requirements
questions.e: The three main NFR categories are System/Product Quality requirements, Design constraints (also called Process Requirements), and Commercial constraints. Business/user/system are the levels of requirements, and speed/size/reliability are measurable NFR properties.

questions.q: Which items fall under the System/Product Quality category of non-functional requirements?
o: Performance, capacity, robustness, usability, reliability, maintainability, and security
Inputs, outputs, and computations
Programming language, database, and platform choices
Cost, delivery date, and development methodology
questions.e: System/Product Quality requirements characterize system properties such as expected performance, capacity, robustness, usability, reliability, maintainability, and security. Cost and delivery date fall under Commercial constraints, and language/database/platform choices fall under Design constraints.

questions.q: Cost and delivery date are classified under which non-functional requirement category?
o: Domain requirements
System/Product Quality requirements
Design constraints (Process Requirements)
Commercial constraints
questions.e: Cost and delivery date fall under Commercial constraints, which constrain the project plan and development methods and are often put in a contract or project plan instead. Design constraints instead concern how the system is designed and built.

questions.q: In the table of measurable NFRs, which measures are associated with the Reliability property?
o: Percentage of target-dependent statements and number of target systems
Training time and number of help frames
Processed transactions per second and screen refresh time
Mean time to failure, probability of unavailability, rate of failure occurrence, and availability
questions.e: Reliability is measured by mean time to failure, probability of unavailability, rate of failure occurrence, and availability. Transactions per second measure speed, training time measures ease of use, and target-dependent statements measure portability.

questions.q: Which measures are used for the Portability property in the measurable NFR table?
o: K Bytes and number of help frames
Time to restart after failure and percentage of events causing failure
Percentage of target-dependent statements and number of target systems
Processed transactions per second and user response time
questions.e: Portability is measured by the percentage of target-dependent statements and the number of target systems. Restart time and percentage of events causing failure measure robustness, while K Bytes and help frames measure size.

questions.q: Where do application domain requirements originate?
o: From the commercial constraints of the project
From the application domain, reflecting characteristics and features of that domain
From the software requirements specification
From the funding sponsor and marketing department
questions.e: Application domain requirements are derived from the application domain and describe system characteristics and features that reflect the domain. They may be new functional requirements, constraints on existing requirements, or specific computations; if not satisfied, the system may be unworkable.

questions.q: What are the two main challenges identified with domain requirements?
o: Understandability and implicitness
Reliability and robustness
Cost and delivery date
Performance and portability
questions.e: The challenges are understandability (requirements expressed in the application-domain language that software engineers may not understand) and implicitness (domain specialists know the area so well they do not make domain requirements explicit, reflecting tacit knowledge).

questions.q: What is characteristic of emergent properties of a system?
o: They are independent of the system architecture
They depend on how all software components interoperate and only emerge once all subsystems have been integrated
They can be fully addressed by a single component in isolation
They are always documented as functional 'shall' statements
questions.e: Emergent properties are properties of the system as a whole that cannot be addressed by a single component; they depend on how all components interoperate, only emerge after all subsystems are integrated, and depend on the system architecture. Examples include reliability, maintainability, performance, usability, and security & safety.

questions.q: In the library example, 'At least 20 transactions per second should be possible' is classified as which type of requirement?
o: Functional requirement
Security requirement
Availability requirement
Performance requirement
questions.e: This statement is classified as a performance requirement. In the same example, 'All services should be available within 10 minutes' is an availability requirement, and 'Users have no access to personal data of other users' is a security requirement.

questions.q: In the requirement-classification example, the statement that the user interface should be web-based (accessible via a WWW browser) is classified as what?
o: An implementation requirement
A functional requirement
A performance requirement
A security requirement
questions.e: Requiring the user interface to be web-based (accessible via a WWW browser) is classified as an implementation requirement. In the same example, searching by Title, Author, and/or ISDN is the functional requirement.

questions.q: According to the conclusion on requirement derivation, how are software requirements related to system requirements in a system containing software?
o: System requirements are derived from the software requirements
The two are always identical and interchangeable
Software requirements replace the need for system requirements
Software requirements are derived from the system requirements
questions.e: In a system containing software, software requirements are derived from the system requirements. The system may consist of hardware and software, with the hardware, operating system, and existing software modules forming part of the environment in which the software is used.

questions.q: In which situation is analysis of an existing system MOST useful as an elicitation technique?
o: When the development team wants to avoid interviewing any users
When requirements must be fixed without any documentation
When building a new, improved version of an existing system
When no comparable system has ever existed in the domain
questions.e: Analysing an existing system is especially useful when building a new, improved version of that system, because it reveals what is used, unused, or missing, what works well, and how the system is actually used versus how it was intended to be used.

questions.q: One reason given for analysing an existing system before replacing it is the risk that users may resist a system that is too different. What is this risk called?
o: The Yes, But syndrome
Nostalgia for the old system
The Undiscovered Ruins syndrome
Statistical significance bias
questions.e: Users may become disillusioned with a new system if it is too different or does not do what they want, described as the risk of nostalgia for the old system. This motivates analysing real usage patterns of the existing system.

questions.q: Document review as an elicitation starting point may include user manuals, development documents, requirements documents, internal memos, and which additional source?
o: Marketing brochures
Change histories
Competitor advertisements
Stakeholder salaries
questions.e: Document review starts with available documentation including user documents, development documents, requirements documents, internal memos, and change histories, even though such documents are often out of date, poorly written, or wrong.

questions.q: When first observing a user at work as an elicitation technique, what is the recommended initial approach?
o: Observe silently at first, otherwise you may get biased information
Avoid recording anything to prevent distraction
Immediately interrupt to ask detailed design questions
Explain to the user what they are doing wrong as they work
questions.e: In observation, you should initially observe silently, otherwise you may get biased information; the user is then asked to explain everything they are doing, and sessions may be videotaped.

questions.q: The term 'ethnography' comes from anthropology and literally means what?
o: Writing the culture
Observing the interface
Measuring the goal
Studying the machine
questions.e: Ethnography comes from anthropology and literally means 'writing the culture.' It is borrowed from social science, using observation of human activity and the work environment to inform the study of a phenomenon.

questions.q: How does ethnographic observation differ from a technique where the user is asked to explain their actions?
o: In ethnography, the observer must remain completely hidden from workers
In ethnography, only questionnaires are used and no watching occurs
In ethnography, discoveries come from observation and analysis, and workers are not asked to explain what they do
In ethnography, workers write their own requirements documents
questions.e: In ethnography, discoveries are made by observation and analysis, and workers are not asked to explain what they do; the aim is to collect the ordinary and make the implicit explicit by studying the context of work.

questions.q: Ethnography can be supplemented later with questionnaires primarily to achieve what?
o: Eliminate the need for any follow-up interviews
Replace all direct observation of the workplace
Guarantee that political factors are fully explored
Answer questions needing comparison or corroboration and obtain statistics from a large number of users
questions.e: Ethnography can be supplemented with questionnaires to answer questions that need comparison or corroboration (confirmation) and to obtain statistics from a large number of users, looking for statistical significance.

questions.q: Ethnographic observation is described as LESS useful for exploring which of the following?
o: What a technician physically does during the day
Political factors, because workers are aware of an outside observer's presence
The ordinary, everyday activities of workers
What a worker's workspace looks like
questions.e: Ethnography is useful for discovering everyday activities and workspaces, but it is less useful for exploring political factors because workers are aware of the presence of an outside observer.

questions.q: In the air traffic control ethnography example, why did the controllers repeatedly close the system's audible conflict alarm?
o: The alarm was broken and produced no sound
They were annoyed by the constant warnings, having intentionally set conflicting headings to fix later
They had never been trained on what the alarm meant
The alarm only sounded when there was no real conflict
questions.e: Controllers often put aircraft on potentially conflicting headings intending to fix them later; the system sounded an audible alarm on possible conflict, and the controllers closed the alarms because they were annoyed by the constant warnings.

questions.q: During interviews, why should detailed, solution-specific questions be used cautiously?
o: They cannot be recorded in elicitation notes
They prevent interviewing more than one person
They always take too long to answer
They may miss the stakeholder's real requirements
questions.e: Detailed and solution-specific questions may miss the stakeholder's real requirements. For example, asking 'Would you like Word 2007, Excel 2007, or both?' is worse than the problem-oriented 'Would you like to do word processing, computations, or both?'

questions.q: The interviewing process is described as consisting of four important steps. Which sequence correctly lists them?
o: Observation, ethnography, questionnaires, interviews
Planning and preparation, interview session, consolidation of information, follow-up
Brainstorming, storming, calming, voting
Goal setting, questioning, measuring, reporting
questions.e: The interview process consists of four steps: planning and preparation, the interview session, consolidation of information, and follow-up.

questions.q: Interviewing several people at once is recommended in order to create what effect?
o: Corroboration, where statistics reach significance
Synergy, where the combined action of things exceeds the sum of individual effects
Redundancy, where every answer is repeated for accuracy
Fidelity, where responses become more reactive
questions.e: Interviewing several people at once creates synergy, the phenomenon in which the combined action of two or more things is greater than the sum of their individual effects; group responses outperform the sum of individual responses.

questions.q: Which of the following is identified as a common interviewing mistake?
o: Revising elicitation notes soon after the interview
Using the interviewee's own terminology
Asking direct questions too early instead of indirect ones
Interviewing people in small groups to create synergy
questions.e: Asking direct questions too early is a common interviewing mistake. For example, asking 'How much horsepower do you need?' directly is worse than the indirect 'How many passengers? How far? How fast?'

questions.q: The advice 'often users do not know exactly what they want, so narrow what is asked for down to what is needed' addresses which interviewing mistake?
o: Trying to convince stakeholders that you are smart
Assuming that stated needs are exactly correct
Interviewing one-at-a-time instead of in small groups
Not interviewing all of the right people
questions.e: Assuming that stated needs are exactly correct is a mistake because users often do not know exactly what they want; the interviewer must narrow what is asked for down to what is actually needed.

questions.q: Regarding elicitation notes taken during interviews, why should they be revised and completed soon after the interview?
o: Because one quickly forgets the details and everything else
Because notes cannot legally be kept overnight
Because the interviewee must approve them within one hour
Because diagrams and charts must be discarded immediately
questions.e: Elicitation notes should be revised and completed soon after the interview because one forgets the details (and everything else); inconsistencies should be identified and addressed in follow-up, and the interviewee's terminology should be used.

questions.q: Brainstorming is recommended as an elicitation technique particularly in which circumstance?
o: When the goal is to obtain statistics from a large user base
Early in a project when terrain is uncertain, expertise is scarce, and innovation is important
Only when a single, well-understood idea already exists
Late in a project when all requirements are already fixed and stable
questions.e: Brainstorming is used to invent new ways of doing things when much is unknown, especially early in a project when the terrain is uncertain, there is little expertise for the type of application, and innovation is important.

questions.q: Brainstorming consists of two main activities, 'The Storm' and 'The Calm.' What is the goal of The Storm?
o: Filtering ideas down to the best one(s) through voting
Generating as many ideas as possible, valuing quantity not quality
Assigning weighted scores to each acceptance criterion
Writing the final ranked requirements document
questions.e: The Storm generates as many ideas as possible, where quantity, not quality, is the goal and 'wild is good,' while The Calm filters ideas by combining, clarifying, prioritising, and improving to keep the best one(s).

questions.q: In brainstorming roles, what constraint applies to the moderator/leader?
o: The moderator must be an external ideas-person only
The moderator must remain completely silent
The moderator must also record every idea personally
The moderator cannot also be the scribe
questions.e: The moderator/leader cannot be the scribe. There are two schools of thought: the 'traffic cop' who enforces rules of order, and the 'agent provocateur' who additionally takes a leadership role and comes prepared with wild ideas to present for discussion.

questions.q: In brainstorming, what distinguishes the 'agent provocateur' moderator from the 'traffic cop' moderator?
o: The agent provocateur never speaks and only enforces order
The agent provocateur eliminates all ideas before discussion
The agent provocateur takes a leadership role and comes prepared with wild ideas to present
The agent provocateur acts as the scribe writing down ideas
questions.e: A traffic cop enforces rules of order without throwing weight around, whereas an agent provocateur is a traffic cop plus more of a leadership role, coming prepared with wild ideas and explicitly looking for variations and combinations.

questions.q: In the 'voting with threshold' method used to eliminate brainstorming ideas, how is voting structured?
o: Only the moderator votes, using a weighted formula
Each person casts exactly one vote and the single top idea wins
Voting is forbidden and blending ideas is the only method
Each person votes up to n times, ideas with more than m votes are kept, and multiple rounds use smaller n and m
questions.e: In voting with threshold, each person is allowed to vote up to n times, ideas with more than m votes are kept, and multiple rounds are held with smaller n and m. Voting with campaign speeches is an alternative.

questions.q: Creative or technical brainstorming meetings are noted to lose focus after roughly what duration?
o: 15 to 30 minutes
3 to 4 hours
90 to 120 minutes
45 to 60 minutes
questions.e: During The Calm, meetings (especially creative or technical ones) tend to lose focus after 90 to 120 minutes, so it is advised to take breaks or reconvene later.

questions.q: How is a software requirements prototype defined?
o: A replicate or partial implementation of a software system
A complete, final production release of the software
A written mission statement decomposed into goals
A questionnaire distributed to a large number of users
questions.e: A software requirements prototype is a replicate or partial implementation of a software system that helps developers, users, and customers better understand, clarify, and complete requirements.

questions.q: Prototyping is said to provide an early response to which user attitude?
o: The 'quantity, not quality' attitude
The 'nostalgia for the old system' attitude
The 'I'll know it when I see it (or won't see it)' attitude
The 'writing the culture' attitude
questions.e: Prototyping provides an early response to the 'I'll know it when I see (or won't see) it' attitude and is effective in addressing the 'Yes, But' and the 'Undiscovered Ruins' syndromes.

questions.q: Which pair correctly describes the difference between evolutionary and throw-away prototypes?
o: Evolutionary is static and not operated; throw-away is always high-fidelity
Evolutionary is discarded after use; throw-away becomes the final product
Evolutionary is turned into a product incrementally from well-understood requirements; throw-away is less precise and focuses on less well-understood aspects to elicit or validate requirements
Evolutionary focuses on one layer only; throw-away is a vertical slice of the real system
questions.e: An evolutionary prototype is turned into a product incrementally and begins with requirements that are more understood, giving users a working system more quickly, while a throw-away prototype is less precise, is discarded, and focuses on less well-understood aspects to elicit or validate requirements.

questions.q: In prototyping, what distinguishes a horizontal prototype from a vertical prototype?
o: Horizontal focuses on one layer such as the user interface; vertical is a slice of the real system
Horizontal is static; vertical is reactive and high-fidelity
Horizontal is always thrown away; vertical always evolves into the product
Horizontal is a slice of the real system; vertical focuses only on the user interface
questions.e: A horizontal prototype focuses on one layer, for example the user interface, whereas a vertical prototype is a slice of the real system that cuts through multiple layers.

questions.q: In prototyping, what does 'fidelity' refer to?
o: The number of layers included in the prototype
The number of stakeholders who reviewed the prototype
The cost of programming the prototype
The extent to which the prototype is real and, especially, reactive
questions.e: Fidelity is the extent to which the prototype is real and especially reactive. High-fidelity prototypes 'work' when you press a button, while low-fidelity prototypes are static and not operated.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a DISADVANTAGE of high-fidelity prototypes?
o: They can give a false sense of security and often focus on details rather than goals
They may seem non-professional to some stakeholders
