They may not cover all aspects of interfaces
They are not interactive and cannot be operated
questions.e: High-fidelity prototypes take time and money to build, can be difficult to change, give a false sense of security, and often focus on details rather than goals and important issues. Being static, non-interactive, or seeming non-professional are disadvantages of low-fidelity prototypes.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as an ADVANTAGE of low-fidelity prototypes?
o: They are easy and quick to build, cheaper to develop, and engage users before coding begins
They reduce design risk through executable modeling
They give a strong understanding of full functionality
They provide more precise verdicts about requirements
questions.e: Low-fidelity prototypes are easy and quick to build, cheaper to develop, excellent for interfaces, engage users before coding begins, and encourage creativity. Understanding functionality, precise verdicts, and reduced design risk are advantages of high-fidelity prototypes.

questions.q: Which risk of prototyping is specifically mentioned regarding user-interface-focused prototypes?
o: They always become part of the production system
They tend to lose the focus of demonstrating or exploring functionality
They prevent any user participation in the project
They make customers' expectations unrealistically low
questions.e: Prototypes that focus on the user interface tend to lose the focus of demonstrating or exploring functionality; other risks include raising customer expectations about completion unrealistically and mistaking a throwaway prototype for part of the production system.

questions.q: In goal-based approaches, from where are requirements recognized to emanate?
o: From direct observation of workers who are not asked to explain their actions
From a replicate or partial implementation of the system
From the mission statement, through a set of goals that lead to requirements
From the largest number of votes cast in a brainstorming session
questions.e: Goal-based approaches comprise techniques in which requirements are recognized to emanate from the mission statement through a set of goals, which are then decomposed into requirements using a structured approach such as goal-question-metric (GQM).

questions.q: The GQM technique incorporates three steps. Which sequence correctly orders them?
o: State the objectives or goals, derive the questions that determine if each goal is met, then decide what to measure
Observe the work, interview the workers, then build a prototype
Measure the system, form questions about the measurements, then set goals from them
Generate ideas, filter ideas, then vote on the best idea
questions.e: GQM (Basili and Weiss 1984) has three steps: state the system's objectives or goals, derive from each goal the questions that must be answered to determine if the goal is met, and decide what must be measured in order to answer those questions.

questions.q: Who is credited with developing the use case technique for describing sequences of interactions between a system and external actors?
o: Sindre and Opdahl
Ivar Jacobson
Ham and Larman
Awais Majeed
questions.e: Use cases were developed by Ivar Jacobson, and the technique is not exclusively for Object Oriented Analysis. Sindre and Opdahl are associated with misuse cases, while Ham and Larman are cited for alternative ways of identifying use cases.

questions.q: What is an actor in the context of use case modeling?
o: A unique label used to reference a use case elsewhere
A computation the system performs internally
Any agent that interacts with the system to achieve a useful goal, such as people, other software systems, or hardware
A specific occurrence of a use case at a specific time with specific data
questions.e: An actor is any agent that interacts with the system to achieve a useful goal, including people, other software systems, and hardware. A specific occurrence with specific data describes a scenario, and a unique label is the use case's identifier.

questions.q: A use case should primarily describe which of the following?
o: The physical hardware components of the system
The computations the system performs internally
The user's interaction with the system, covering the full sequence of steps from the beginning of a task until the end
The class hierarchy and inheritance structure of the system
questions.e: A use case should describe the user's interaction with the system, not the computations the system performs, and generally should cover the full sequence of steps from the beginning of a task until the end.

questions.q: Which type of use case is described as abstract, technology free, and implementation independent, defined at earlier stages?
o: Concrete use case
Essential use case
Negative use case
Misuse case
questions.e: Essential use cases are abstract, technology free, and implementation independent, defined at earlier stages (e.g., customer identifies him/herself). Concrete use cases are technology/user interface dependent (e.g., customer inserts a card, types a PIN).

questions.q: In the UML/UC community, how is a scenario best defined?
o: A set of use cases plus an optional description of how they relate
A hostile agent's goal that threatens the system
An instance of a use case expressing a specific occurrence (a specific path) with a specific actor, time, and data
A unique label used to reference a use case
questions.e: A scenario is an instance of a use case that expresses a specific occurrence, a specific path through the use case, involving a specific actor, at a specific time, and with specific data. Many scenarios may be generated from a single use case description.

questions.q: How many primary and secondary scenarios does a use case include?
o: 1 primary scenario and 0 or more secondary scenarios
0 or more primary and 0 or more secondary scenarios
Exactly 1 primary and exactly 1 secondary scenario
0 or more primary scenarios and exactly 1 secondary scenario
questions.e: A use case includes 1 primary scenario (the normal course of events) and 0 or more secondary scenarios (alternative/exceptional courses of events that are variations of the primary scenario).

questions.q: How does an alternative scenario differ from an exceptional scenario?
o: An alternative scenario is technology dependent, while an exceptional scenario is technology free
An alternative scenario handles error conditions, while an exceptional scenario is the normal course of events
Both describe identical situations with no meaningful difference
An alternative scenario meets the intent of the use case but with a different sequence of steps, while an exceptional scenario addresses conditions differing from the norm and cases already covered
questions.e: An alternative scenario meets the intent of the use case but with a different sequence of steps, whereas an exceptional scenario addresses conditions of the main and alternative cases that differ from the norm and from cases already covered.

questions.q: Which scenario type is used to describe a current situation, typically in re-engineering projects describing the existing system?
o: Visionary (TO-BE) scenario
Evaluation scenario
Training scenario
AS-IS scenario
questions.e: An AS-IS scenario describes a current situation and is usually used in re-engineering projects describing the current system. A Visionary (TO-BE) scenario describes a future improved system, while an evaluation scenario provides user tasks for evaluating the system.

questions.q: Which scenario type provides step-by-step instructions that guide a novice user through a system?
o: Visionary scenario
AS-IS scenario
Training scenario
Evaluation scenario
questions.e: A training scenario gives step-by-step instructions that guide a novice user through a system. An evaluation scenario instead provides user tasks against which the system is to be evaluated.

questions.q: What does an <<include>> relationship between two use cases primarily enable?
o: Threatening the system from a hostile agent's viewpoint
Defining an is-a relationship between actors
Making optional interactions explicit or handling exceptional cases
Expressing commonality between several different use cases so details are not repeated, enabling reuse and consistency
questions.e: Inclusions allow one to express commonality between several different use cases; even very different use cases can share a sequence of actions (reuse), avoiding repeating details (consistency). Making optional interactions explicit is the role of <<extend>>.

questions.q: Which statement about the relationship between a base use case and its included use case is correct?
o: The base use case cannot exist without the included use case, and when the included use case is done, control returns to the base use case
Control never returns to the base use case once the included use case begins
The included use case cannot be shared with any other use case
The base use case can exist without the included use case
questions.e: For inclusions, the base use case references the included use case as needed and cannot exist without it; when the included use case is done, control returns to the base use case. A stated disadvantage is having to look in multiple places to understand the use case.

questions.q: What is the stated disadvantage of using inclusions?
o: You have to look in multiple places to understand the use case
There is disagreement over the semantics
The base use case can no longer be executed on its own
Extension points must be created explicitly
questions.e: The disadvantage of inclusions is that you have to look in multiple places to understand the use case. Disagreement over semantics and explicit extension points are associated with <<extend>> relationships instead.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of the <<extend>> relationship?
o: To express an is-a relationship between two use cases
To decompose a complex task into a lower-level task with a lower-level goal
To make optional interactions explicit or to handle exceptional cases while keeping the basic use case description simple
To indicate that a misuse case threatens a use case
questions.e: The <<extend>> relationship is used to make optional interactions explicit or to handle exceptional cases; by creating separate extensions the basic use case remains simple, and the base use case can still execute without the extension. It should be used sparingly due to semantic disagreement.

questions.q: Which statement is true regarding a base use case and its <<extend>> extension?
o: The base use case cannot be executed without the extension
Extension points are created automatically without any effort
The base use case can still be executed without the use case extension, and extension points must be created explicitly in the base use case
When the extension is done, the base use case is terminated
questions.e: With <<extend>>, the base use case can still be executed without the extension, and extension points must be created explicitly in the base use case. This contrasts with inclusions, where the base use case cannot exist without the included use case.

questions.q: For which element is generalization noted as being particularly useful and clearer, as opposed to being of unclear semantics?
o: Preconditions
Extension points
Use cases
Actors
questions.e: Generalization is particularly useful and clearer for actors, unlike use case generalization where the semantics are unclear and should be used with caution. Generalization applies to both use cases and actors and requires an is-a relation.

questions.q: In a descriptive use case, what is the suggested form for the Name field?
o: A unique alphanumeric identifier
A full narrative paragraph
Verb object (e.g., Order a product)
Noun-noun construction
questions.e: The Name should succinctly state the user task independently of structure or implementation, with the suggested form being verb object (e.g., Order a product). A unique label instead corresponds to the Identifier field.

questions.q: In a descriptive use case, which field is defined as the state of the system after completion regardless of outcome?
o: Postconditions
Goal
Minimal guarantee
Preconditions
questions.e: The Minimal guarantee is the state of the system after completion regardless of outcome. Postconditions describe the state of the system after completion of the use case, while preconditions state what must be satisfied before it can begin.

questions.q: How is the primary actor distinguished from participants (secondary actors) in a use case description?
o: The primary actor only observes, while participants initiate the use case
The primary actor is a hostile agent, while participants are friendly agents
The primary actor is always a hardware device, while participants are always people
The primary actor initiates the use case, while participants provide services and interact with the system after the use case was initiated
questions.e: The primary actor initiates the use case, whereas participants (secondary actors) are other actors that provide services to the system and interact with it after the use case has been initiated.

questions.q: Which three use case description formats for the description of events are named?
o: State, Sequence, Activity
Essential, Concrete, Abstract
AS-IS, TO-BE, Evaluation
Narrative, Simple column, Multiple columns
questions.e: The description of events (scenarios) can use different formats: Narrative, Simple column, and Multiple columns. The multiple column form uses one column per actor to allow a more detailed view.

questions.q: Which use case description format uses one column per actor to allow a more detailed view?
o: Narrative form
Simple column form
Multiple column form
Storyboard form
questions.e: The multiple column form uses one column per actor (for example, a User's Action column and a System Responses column), allowing for a more detailed view. The narrative form is a paragraph, and the simple column form uses linear numbered sequences.

questions.q: When identifying actors' names, which guideline is recommended?
o: Names should reflect actual specific people rather than roles
Names should reflect roles rather than actual people, using the right level of abstraction
Names should be tied to the organization's paper forms
Names should include situation-specific data
questions.e: Actor names should reflect roles rather than actual people and use the right level of abstraction. For example, 'Pension Clerk' is a good actor name while 'Clerk #1' is a poor one, since an actor specifies a role an external entity adopts.

questions.q: In the ATM Withdraw Cash example, what were identified as the preconditions before the use case can be invoked?
o: The Customer has left with the amount
System is in operation, Cash is available
The card is valid and the PIN is entered
The Registrar is logged into the system
questions.e: For the Withdraw Cash use case, the identified preconditions are that the system is in operation and cash is available. Preconditions are conditions that must be met before invocation of the use case.

questions.q: When looking for secondary scenarios, which question corresponds to finding an exception scenario?
o: Is there some behavior that could happen at any time?
Is there some other action that can be taken at this point?
Is there something that could go wrong at this point?
Is there a way to reuse this behavior in another use case?
questions.e: Asking 'Is there something that could go wrong at this point?' finds an exception scenario. Asking whether some other action can be taken finds an alternate scenario, and asking about behavior that could happen at any time finds an alternative scenario (unless it is an error).

questions.q: According to the use case development rules of thumb, which statement reflects the recommended emphasis?
o: The use case diagram is the most important part, so spend most time on it
The textual description is the most important part; do not spend too much time on the use case diagram
The user interface should be described in detail
Deep hierarchies with <<includes>> should be encouraged
questions.e: A rule of thumb states that the textual description is the most important part and that you should not spend too much time on the use case diagram. Other rules include avoiding functional decomposition and not describing the user interface.

questions.q: According to the rules of thumb, how long should the main flow of a use case ideally be?
o: It should span at least five pages
It should match the length of the full requirements specification
It should fit on a single page
It should describe every possible variation exhaustively
questions.e: The rule 'keep it short, keep it simple' states the main flow should fit on a single page, and cautions against over-specifying behavior. If there are too many use cases, too much detail has probably been included.

questions.q: How is a negative scenario characterized?
o: A training sequence for novice users
Undesirable from the business organization's viewpoint but desirable from a hostile agent's viewpoint (not necessarily human)
A normal happy-day scenario where everything goes fine
Desirable from the business organization's viewpoint and undesirable to a hostile agent
questions.e: A negative scenario has a goal that is undesirable from the business organization's viewpoint but desirable from a hostile agent's viewpoint, where the hostile agent is not necessarily human. Such scenarios should be considered beforehand along with potential solutions.

questions.q: Who proposed misuse cases, and in what year?
o: Ivar Jacobson in 2000
Sindre and Opdahl in 2000
Sindre and Opdahl in 1995
Ham and Larman in 2000
questions.e: Misuse cases were proposed by Sindre and Opdahl in 2000 to capture use cases a system must be protected against, with the goal of threatening the system and obvious applications for security and risk analysis.

questions.q: What is the actor of a misuse case called, and how is it depicted?
o: A primary actor, a friendly agent, drawn as a stick figure
A misactor, a hostile agent, with the colors of the ellipse inverted
An installation technician, drawn with a bold ellipse
A secondary actor, drawn with a dashed ellipse
questions.e: The misuse case's misactor is a hostile agent, and the colors of the ellipse are inverted to distinguish it from a normal use case. A misactor wants to harm the system or achieve goals incompatible with the system's goals.

questions.q: Which two new relations are introduced with misuse cases, and in which direction do they run?
o: generalizes (actor to actor) and associates (actor to use case)
includes (base to included) and extends (extension to base)
threatens (use case to misuse case) and mitigates (misuse case to use case)
threatens (misuse case to use case) and mitigates (use case to misuse case)
questions.e: Misuse cases introduce two new relations: threatens, which runs from a misuse case to a use case, and mitigates, which runs from a use case to a misuse case. This is likened to a chess match where the best move is to counter the opponent's best move.

questions.q: In the three-step process for finding misuse cases, what happens in Step 3?
o: Find misuse cases and add the threaten relationship
Find misactors (hostile roles)
Mitigate misuse cases by asking what would neutralize the threats, possibly adding a new included use case, extension, or secondary scenario
Determine candidate system scope and boundaries
questions.e: In Step 3, misuse cases are mitigated by asking what would neutralize the threats; a new included use case, new extension use case, or new secondary scenario may be added. Step 1 finds misactors and Step 2 finds misuse cases and adds the threaten relationship.

questions.q: What is identified as a risk of using misuse cases, specifically in the mitigation step?
o: Documentation of rationales
Elicitation of security and safety requirements
Early identification of test cases
Getting into premature design solutions in step 3 (mitigation) when the goal should be to find requirements
questions.e: A stated risk is getting into premature design solutions in step 3 (mitigation), when the goal should instead be to find requirements such as safety and security. Early test case identification and documentation of rationales are listed as benefits, not risks.

questions.q: In the University Registration System example, the use case 'Enroll Family Member of Staff' (UC-20) relates to 'Enroll in University' (UC-19) through which mechanism?
o: It includes UC-19
It inherits from UC-19
It extends UC-19
It threatens UC-19
questions.e: UC-20 Enroll Family Member of Staff is marked 'Inherits From: UC-19', making it a generalization/specialization; it prepares a bill based on the staff family members rate rather than the standard flow. This illustrates use case generalization rather than include or extend.

questions.q: What is described as one of the goals of requirements elicitation?
o: To determine the sources of information and the appropriate techniques for gathering it
To deliver working software to the customer
To produce a final, complete and consistent specification before any analysis
To eliminate the need for stakeholder involvement
questions.e: A stated elicitation goal is to determine sources of information and appropriate techniques, alongside gathering information on the domain, problem and constraints. The first document produced is expected to be potentially incomplete, disorganized and inconsistent, not final and complete.

questions.q: How is the first document produced during elicitation characterized?
o: A finalized Software Requirements Specification ready for sign-off
Complete, organized and consistent
Mainly user requirements and elicitation notes that may be incomplete, disorganized and inconsistent
Purely a cost-and-schedule estimate
questions.e: The first document consists mainly of user requirements and elicitation notes, and is described as potentially incomplete, disorganized and inconsistent, with the reasoning that 'we must start somewhere'.

questions.q: Under the 'Scope' challenge of elicitation, which problem is identified?
o: Experts are seldom available
Stakeholders refuse to commit to written requirements
System boundaries are inadequately defined or defined too soon
A common vocabulary is often missing
questions.e: The Scope challenge covers system boundaries being inadequately defined or defined too soon, and the inclusion of unnecessary technical details. Refusal to commit belongs to Volatility, while missing vocabulary and unavailable experts are listed as other typical issues.

questions.q: The elicitation challenge of 'Volatility' refers to which situation?
o: System boundaries defined too soon
A lack of understanding of computing capabilities
Stakeholders will not commit to a set of written requirements
Requirements being sometimes too obvious or implicit
questions.e: Volatility is characterized by stakeholders not committing to a set of written requirements. Boundary issues fall under Scope, and being too obvious/implicit falls under the point that requirements do not fall from the sky.

questions.q: The 'Lack of understanding' challenge in elicitation is said to lead to what?
o: Unnecessary technical details
Conflicting requirements and communication issues
Stakeholders refusing to sign off
Experts being seldom available
questions.e: Lack of understanding of what is needed (computing capabilities and limitations, and the domain) leads to conflicting requirements and communication issues.

questions.q: The statement 'Requirements do not fall from the sky!' is used to make which point?
o: Requirements should be defined as early as possible
Requirements are sometimes hidden and sometimes too obvious, implicit or ordinary
Requirements must always be documented in writing
Requirements always require expert consultants
questions.e: The phrase emphasizes that requirements are sometimes hidden and sometimes too obvious, implicit or ordinary, meaning they must be actively drawn out rather than expected to appear on their own.

questions.q: In the argument attributed to Prof. Dan Berry, why is ignorance of a domain considered a good thing?
o: It speeds up the writing of the specification
It reduces the cost of hiring domain experts
It allows one to expose hypotheses and some implicit facts
It prevents stakeholders from changing their minds
questions.e: The 'Ignorance is a bliss' point holds that ignorance (not stupidity) allows a requirements engineer to expose hypotheses and implicit facts, with Berry even suggesting engineers might one day advertise their domains of ignorance to find work.

questions.q: What is the correct grouping of the three main phases of the elicitation tasks?
o: Analysis, specification, verification
Objectives, strategies, and products
Planning, during the elicitation, and following the elicitation
Interviews, brainstorming, and questionnaires
questions.e: The tasks performed as part of elicitation are organized into three phases: planning for the elicitation, during the elicitation, and following the elicitation.

questions.q: Which activity is listed as part of the 'during the elicitation' phase?
o: Analyse results to understand obtained information
Record results in the requirements specification
Examine the viability of the project
Negotiate a coherent set of requirements acceptable by all stakeholders
questions.e: During the elicitation, tasks include examining the project's viability, understanding the problem from each stakeholder's perspective, extracting the essence of requirements, and inventing better ways to work. Negotiating, recording and analysing results all belong to the 'following the elicitation' phase.

questions.q: Which of the following is described as a task performed 'following the elicitation'?
o: Negotiate a coherent set of requirements and establish priorities
Examine whether the project is worth it
Invent better ways to do the work of the user
Understand the problem from each stakeholder's perspective
questions.e: The 'following the elicitation' phase includes analysing results, negotiating a coherent set of requirements acceptable to all stakeholders while establishing priorities, and recording results in the requirements specification.

questions.q: Elicitation is best characterized as which kind of activity?
o: A final step performed only after specification and verification
An incremental activity, repeated as needed and driven by the information obtained
A purely automated process requiring no iteration
A one-time, sequential step completed before analysis begins
questions.e: Elicitation is incremental, repeated as needed and driven by the information obtained; a bit of elicitation, analysis, specification and verification are always done at the same time.

questions.q: Which set of items should an Elicitation Plan include?
o: Only a schedule and a budget
Source code, test cases, deployment scripts, user manuals
Purpose, business advantage, cost vs. benefits, feasibility
Objectives; strategies and processes; products; schedule and resource estimates; risks
questions.e: The Elicitation Plan should include objectives, strategies and processes, products of elicitation efforts, schedule and resource estimates, and risks. Purpose, business advantage and feasibility instead belong to examining project viability.

questions.q: When setting elicitation strategies and processes, what does the material recommend regarding approaches such as surveys, workshops and interviews?
o: Avoid workshops because experts are seldom available
Use only questionnaires to save time
Often combine approaches depending on the types and number of stakeholders
Always use a single approach for consistency
questions.e: Elicitation often uses a combination of approaches depending on the types and number of stakeholders, for example surveys (questionnaires), workshops and interviews.

questions.q: In examining project viability, what does the point 'It's very difficult to cancel a project once started' support?
o: That developers are always outsiders
That it is important to check whether the project makes good business sense early
That elicitation should be skipped for small projects
That constraints should be imposed as early as possible
questions.e: Because it is very difficult to cancel a project once started, examining project viability asks whether the project makes good business sense, based on purpose, business advantage, costs vs. benefits, feasibility, scope, required resources, constraints and risks.

questions.q: What distinction does the material draw between technical feasibility and economic feasibility?
o: Technical feasibility concerns skills to build and operate the product, while economic feasibility concerns resources such as time, money and staff
Technical feasibility concerns market data, while economic feasibility concerns scope
Technical feasibility concerns budget, while economic feasibility concerns skills
Both concern only the availability of staff
questions.e: Technical feasibility asks whether the organization has the skills needed to build and operate the product; economic feasibility asks whether it has the resources (time, money, staff) to construct it. In either case, if not, stop the project.

questions.q: Regarding scope when defining a problem for cost and time estimates, which guidance is given?
o: Include as much as possible to be safe
Leave the system boundaries undefined
Exclude as much as possible to reduce the complexity of the problem
Never establish broader goals under any circumstances
questions.e: For cost and time estimates, the advice is to define the problem more precisely, list all the things the system should do, exclude as much as possible to reduce complexity, and establish broader goals only if the problem is too simple.

questions.q: How does the material contrast the 'product vision' with the 'scope' for a single project?
o: Both refer only to the concerns of the Project Manager
The scope affects multiple projects, while the product vision is limited to one release
The product vision may affect multiple projects and evolves slowly, while the scope defines clear limits on what to implement for a single project
The product vision changes rapidly, while the scope never changes
questions.e: The product vision describes the kind of product it should be, may affect multiple projects and evolves relatively slowly, whereas the scope for a single project defines and communicates clear limits on what to implement and is important for the Project Manager.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as an example of a solution constraint?
o: Un-measurable requirements
Mandated COTS (commercial off-the-shelf) components
Hostile stakeholders
Fragile agreement on goals
questions.e: Solution constraints include mandated designs, mandated interacting systems, and mandated COTS (commercial off-the-shelf) components. Hostile stakeholders and fragile agreement are cited as risks, not solution constraints.

questions.q: What advice is given about imposing constraints during the elicitation process?
o: Try not to impose constraints on the process, platform or language unnecessarily or prematurely
Never allow any budget or time constraints
Always mandate a specific programming language
Impose constraints on process, platform and language as early as possible
questions.e: The guidance is to try not to impose constraints on the process, platform, or language unnecessarily or prematurely, even though requirements, solution, time and budget constraints all exist.

questions.q: When extracting the essence of stakeholders' requirements by building models, what do gaps in the model behavior indicate?
o: That there may be unknown or ambiguous situations to resolve by asking stakeholders
That the requirements are complete
That the scope has been defined too soon
That the project is economically infeasible
questions.e: Gaps in the model's behavior may indicate unknown or ambiguous situations; models help focus efforts, and these gaps should be resolved by asking the stakeholders, especially users.

questions.q: According to Dean Leffingwell and Don Widrig, which set represents the classic elicitation challenges?
o: The 'Yes, But' syndrome, 'Undiscovered Ruins', the 'User and Developer' syndrome, and 'The sins of your predecessors' syndrome
Purpose, business advantage, feasibility, and scope
Planning, during, following, and repeating
Scope, understanding, volatility, and vocabulary
questions.e: Leffingwell and Widrig's elicitation challenges are the 'Yes, But' syndrome, the 'Undiscovered Ruins' problem, the 'User and Developer' syndrome, and 'The sins of your predecessors' syndrome.

questions.q: The 'Yes, But' syndrome describes which phenomenon?
o: Users remembering broken promises from past projects
Analysts believing they understand user problems better than users
Teams being unable to decide when elicitation is complete
First-time users reacting to a system with 'wow, this is cool' or 'yes, but... wouldn't it be nice...?'
questions.e: The 'Yes, But' syndrome is the human-nature reaction of first-time users, who respond either enthusiastically or with 'yes, but' feedback; it tends to be user-interface centric, so teams should anticipate it and add time and resources for feedback.

questions.q: The 'Undiscovered Ruins' problem in elicitation is analogous to which question?
o: Asking an archaeologist 'how many undiscovered ruins are there?'
'Are stakeholders politically motivated?'
'Do we have the skills to build the product?'
'How much will the product cost to operate?'
questions.e: The 'Undiscovered Ruins' problem captures teams' struggle to know when elicitation is done, likened to asking an archaeologist how many undiscovered ruins there are; the remedy is to first scope the effort by defining the problems to be solved.

questions.q: In the 'User and Developer' syndrome, what response is suggested for the characteristic 'Users think they know what they want until developers give them what they said they wanted'?
o: Recognize and appreciate users as domain experts
Provide alternative elicitation techniques earlier, such as storyboards, role playing and prototypes
Put the analyst in the user's place for an hour or a day
Accept it as human nature and get on with the program
questions.e: For users who only realize their true needs after seeing what they asked for, the suggested response is to provide alternative elicitation techniques earlier, such as storyboards, role playing and prototypes.

questions.q: The 'Living with the Sins' (sins of your predecessors) syndrome recommends which approach?
o: Build trust slowly, avoid over-committing, and deliver highest-priority features early
Delay all deliveries until every requirement is elicited
Over-commit to features to win user confidence
Cut features unilaterally to meet the schedule
questions.e: Because users and developers remember past disappointments such as vague requirements and unilaterally cut features, the advice is to build trust slowly, not over-commit to features, schedule or budget, and build success by delivering highest-priority features early.

questions.q: In the 'Other Factors' discussion, what point is made with 'No system is an island unto itself'?
o: Systems should never depend on interacting systems
Every system must be built with off-the-shelf components
Requirements always fall from the sky
All software systems exist and are used within a particular technical and social context, and social and organizational factors often dominate requirements
questions.e: The phrase stresses that all software systems exist within a particular technical and social context, where social and organizational factors (trust deficit, power politics, authority, transparency, accountability) often dominate the requirements and can be difficult to determine.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a technique for understanding the problem from each stakeholder's point of view?
o: Delivering highest-priority features early
Estimating effort and scheduling resources
Observing the current system, interviews, brainstorming and facilitation
Mandating COTS components
questions.e: Understanding the problem from each stakeholder's perspective uses techniques such as observing the current system, interviews, brainstorming, facilitation, reviewing documentation, questionnaires, identifying context and detecting ambiguities.

questions.q: What does 'Invent better ways to do the user's work' involve?
o: Asking why documented requirements are desired and brainstorming requirements the stakeholders have not yet thought of
Accepting the client's documented requirements without question
Imposing platform and language constraints early
Recording results directly in the SRS without analysis
questions.e: Inventing better ways involves asking why the requirements gathered so far are desired, since the client's view can be limited by past experience, and brainstorming to invent requirements the stakeholders have not yet thought of.

questions.q: What does Quality Function Deployment (QFD) primarily aim to accomplish?
o: Generating source code automatically from a formal requirements specification
Verifying that a delivered system conforms to its architectural design
Estimating project cost and schedule using historical productivity data
Discovering customer requirements and defining major quality assurance points to be used throughout the production phase
questions.e: QFD is defined as a technique for discovering customer requirements and defining major quality assurance points to be used throughout the production phase, distinguishing it from cost estimation or design verification techniques.

questions.q: Who introduced Quality Function Deployment, and in what year?
o: Kano in 1984
Yoji Akao in 1966
Edward Yourdon in 1975
Barry Boehm in 1981
questions.e: QFD was introduced by Yoji Akao in 1966, originally for use in manufacturing, heavy industry, and systems engineering.

questions.q: For which fields was QFD originally introduced before being applied to software?
o: Banking, insurance, and retail
Education, government, and defense
Manufacturing, heavy industry, and systems engineering
Aviation, medicine, and telecommunications
questions.e: QFD was introduced by Yoji Akao in 1966 for use in manufacturing, heavy industry, and systems engineering; it was only later applied to software systems.

questions.q: By what alternative name is QFD often referred to?
o: Voice matrix
Requirements traceability grid
House of quality
Kano model
questions.e: QFD is often referred to as the 'house of quality', which is why an uncontrollably growing feature list is said to turn the house into a 'mansion'.

questions.q: Which perspective does QFD emphasize focusing on?
o: The voice of the competitor's product designers
The 'voice of engineer', not only the 'voice of customer'
The 'voice of customer', not only the 'voice of engineer'
The voice of management above all stakeholders
questions.e: QFD focuses on the 'voice of customer' and not only on the 'voice of engineer', reflecting its goal of discovering genuine customer requirements.

questions.q: What is the basic idea behind QFD?
o: To replace stakeholder interviews with automated surveys
To rank developers by their contribution to each feature
To construct relationship matrices between customer needs, technical requirements, priorities, and (if needed) competitor assessment
To automate acceptance testing through model-based generation
questions.e: The basic idea of QFD is to construct relationship matrices linking customer needs, technical requirements, priorities, and, if needed, competitor assessment.

questions.q: Which set of elicitation and analysis techniques does QFD incorporate?
o: Data flow diagrams, entity models, and state charts
Card sorting, laddering, and domain analysis
Use cases, scenarios, and storyboards
Prototyping, brainstorming, and JAD sessions
questions.e: QFD incorporates card sorting, laddering, and domain analysis as part of its approach to eliciting and structuring requirements.

questions.q: Which companies are cited as having applied QFD to software systems?
o: Oracle, SAP, Adobe, and Intel
Google, Amazon, Facebook, and Netflix
IBM, DEC, HP, AT&T, and Texas Instruments
Microsoft, Apple, Sun, and Cisco
questions.e: QFD, though introduced for manufacturing, was applied to software systems by IBM, DEC, HP, AT&T, Texas Instruments, and others.

questions.q: In the requirements engineering process prescribed by QFD, which activity comes first?
o: Prioritize technical features for development effort
Conduct an evaluation of competing products
Identify the stakeholder's attributes or requirements
Specify a target value for each technical feature
questions.e: The QFD-prescribed process begins by identifying the stakeholder's attributes or requirements, before technical features are identified and related to those requirements.

questions.q: As part of the QFD requirements engineering process, what is specified for each technical feature after evaluation?
o: A responsible development team
A unique identifier
A target value
A risk probability
questions.e: The QFD process calls for evaluating technical features and specifying a target value for each feature, before prioritizing those features for development effort.

questions.q: In QFD's structured approach to competitive analysis, how is the feature list created?
o: Randomly sampled from customer surveys
From the intersection of features shared by all competing products
From the union of all relevant features for competitive products
Only from features of the market-leading product
questions.e: QFD creates the competition feature list from the union of all relevant features across competitive products, helping ensure that key features are not omitted from the new system.

questions.q: In a QFD competition matrix, what do the columns and rows represent?
o: Columns are target values and rows are stakeholders
Columns are customer needs and rows are priorities
Columns are the competing products and rows are the features
Columns are the features and rows are the competing products
questions.e: In the competition matrix, the features comprise the columns while the rows present the competing products, with cells populated for features included in each product.

questions.q: What does the QFD competition matrix provide as a result of populating its cells?
o: A complete work-breakdown structure for development
A cost estimate for each competing product
A ranked list of stakeholders by influence
A starter set of mandatory and optional features
questions.e: The competition matrix gives a starter set of mandatory and optional features and helps ensure key features are not omitted from the new system.

questions.q: Which of the following is identified as an advantage of QFD?
o: It removes the need for measurable target values
It guarantees defect-free requirements specifications
It eliminates the need to evaluate competing products
It shortens the development lifecycle and improves overall project development
questions.e: Among its advantages, QFD shortens the development lifecycle and improves overall project development, in addition to improving user and manager involvement.

questions.q: Which advantage of QFD relates to information management during elicitation?
o: It encrypts stakeholder communications
It compresses all requirements into a single value
It provides a preventive tool that avoids the loss of information
It automatically archives obsolete requirements
questions.e: QFD provides a preventive tool that avoids the loss of information, while also supporting team involvement by structuring communication processes.

questions.q: Which is cited as a drawback of QFD?
o: It cannot involve managers in the process
There may be difficulties in expressing temporal requirements
It forces the development lifecycle to lengthen
It prevents evaluation of competing products
questions.e: A stated drawback of QFD is that there may be difficulties in expressing temporal requirements, alongside challenges with new project types and finding measurements.

questions.q: Why is QFD described as difficult to use with an entirely new project type?
o: Because such projects have too many stakeholders to interview
Because new projects always lack managers to involve
Because it is hard to discover customer requirements for something that does not exist and to build and analyze competitive products, leaving a cognitive gap
Because target values cannot be numeric for new projects
questions.e: For an entirely new project type, it is hard to discover customer requirements for something that does not yet exist and to build and analyze competitive products; looking at similar products still leaves a cognitive gap.

questions.q: According to QFD's drawbacks, what happens when the feature list grows uncontrollably?
o: The competition matrix becomes empty
The development lifecycle automatically shortens
The house of quality can become a 'mansion'
The voice of the customer overrides the voice of the engineer
questions.e: As the feature list grows uncontrollably, the house of quality can become a 'mansion', reflecting the challenge of managing an ever-expanding set of features.

questions.q: Which difficulty is listed among QFD's drawbacks concerning measurement?
o: Every function must be measured in monetary units
Measurements always require competitor cooperation
Measurements can only be taken after deployment
It is sometimes hard to find measurements for certain functions and to keep the level of abstraction uniform
questions.e: A drawback of QFD is that it is sometimes hard to find measurements for certain functions and to keep the level of abstraction uniform across the analysis.

questions.q: What do non-functional requirements primarily define about a system?
o: The overall qualities or attributes of the resulting system
The specific services and functions the system must perform
The individual user tasks the system automates
The step-by-step algorithms the system must implement
questions.e: Non-functional requirements define the overall qualities or attributes of the resulting system, rather than specifying particular functions or services (which functional requirements do).

questions.q: Which of the following best describes what non-functional requirements place on a system?
o: Restrictions on the product, the development process, and external constraints the product must meet
Only the data structures the product must store
A complete list of user-facing features
The exact source code modules to be written
questions.e: NFRs place restrictions on the product being developed and on the development process, and they specify external constraints that the product must meet.

questions.q: Which set of items are given as typical examples of non-functional requirements?
o: Safety, security, usability, reliability and performance
Database, network, storage and CPU
Login, search, reporting and printing
Analysis, design, coding and testing
questions.e: Examples of NFRs include safety, security, usability, reliability and performance requirements. The other lists mix functions, hardware, or lifecycle phases rather than quality attributes.

questions.q: Whether a requirement is expressed as functional or non-functional may depend on which of the following factors?
o: The hardware platform and the operating system
The level of detail in the requirements document and the degree of trust between customer and developer
The programming language and the compiler chosen
The size of the development team and its budget
questions.e: The boundary between functional and non-functional requirements is ambiguous; whether a requirement is expressed one way or the other may depend on the level of detail included in the requirements document and the degree of trust between the system customer and developer.

questions.q: The requirement 'The system shall ensure that data is protected from unauthorised access' is conventionally considered non-functional. What makes it non-functional rather than functional?
o: It cannot be tested in any way
It applies only to the development process
It refers to a natural law such as physics
It does not specify specific system functionality that must be provided
questions.e: This is conventionally a non-functional requirement because it does not specify specific system functionality that must be provided; if it named a login-name-and-password authorisation procedure, it would become functional.

questions.q: 'The system shall include a user authorisation procedure where users must identify themselves using a login name and password, and only authorised users may access the system data.' How is this requirement classified?
o: A non-functional requirement, because it concerns security
A process requirement, because it constrains development
A functional requirement, because it specifies specific system functionality
An external requirement, because it derives from regulations
questions.e: By adding the specific login-name-and-password authorisation procedure, the security concern is expressed as a functional requirement because it now specifies specific system functionality that must be provided.

questions.q: According to a more general classification of NFRs, requirements are distinguished among which three categories?
o: Safety, security and usability requirements
Product, process and external requirements
Performance, capacity and space requirements
Reliability, efficiency and portability requirements
questions.e: One classification is by qualities the software must exhibit (Boehm), while a more general classification distinguishes between product, process and external requirements.

questions.q: The classification of NFRs in terms of qualities that a software must exhibit is attributed to whom?
o: Boehm
Sommerville
ISO 9000
Awais Majeed
questions.e: NFRs may be classified in terms of qualities that a software must exhibit, a classification attributed to Boehm.

questions.q: What do product requirements specify?
o: Constraints on the development process such as CASE tools
The management reports that must be produced
The desired characteristics that a system or subsystem must possess
Regulations derived from the external environment
questions.e: Product requirements specify the desired characteristics that a system or subsystem must possess; most are concerned with constraints on the behaviour of the executing system.

questions.q: Among product requirements, which type can typically be formulated precisely and easily quantified?
o: Safety
Maintainability
Usability
Performance and capacity
questions.e: Some product requirements such as performance and capacity can be formulated precisely and thus easily quantified, whereas others like usability are more difficult to quantify and are often stated informally.

questions.q: Which product requirement is described as often stated informally because it is difficult to quantify?
o: Capacity
Space
Performance
Usability
questions.e: Usability is given as an example of a product requirement that is more difficult to quantify and is consequently often stated informally, in contrast to performance and capacity.

questions.q: 'The System service X shall have an availability of 999/1000 or 99%.' What kind of requirement is this, and what does it mean?
o: A space requirement meaning 999 KB of memory
A portability requirement meaning it runs on 999 platforms
A performance requirement meaning 999 transactions per second
A reliability requirement meaning that out of every 1000 requests, 999 must be satisfied
questions.e: This is a reliability requirement: an availability of 999/1000 means that out of every 1000 requests for the service, 999 must be satisfied.

questions.q: 'System Y shall process a minimum of 8 transactions per second.' This is an example of which type of requirement?
o: A reliability requirement
A performance requirement
A portability requirement
A space requirement
questions.e: A minimum throughput of 8 transactions per second is a performance requirement.

questions.q: 'The executable code of System Z shall be limited to 512 Kbytes.' What type of requirement does this represent?
o: A space requirement specifying the maximum memory size
A reliability requirement
A security requirement
A performance requirement
questions.e: Limiting the executable code to 512 Kbytes is a space requirement, which specifies the maximum memory size of the system.

questions.q: 'The system shall be developed for PC and Macintosh platforms.' This is best classified as which type of product requirement?
o: A security requirement
A performance requirement
A reliability requirement
A portability requirement
questions.e: A requirement to develop the system for both PC and Macintosh platforms is a portability requirement, which affects the way the system may be designed.

questions.q: 'The system must encrypt all external communications using the RSA algorithm.' What type of requirement is this?
o: A portability requirement
A space requirement
A performance requirement
A security requirement specifying that a specific algorithm must be used
questions.e: Requiring encryption of external communications with the RSA algorithm is a security requirement that specifies a specific algorithm must be used in the product.

questions.q: Which example illustrates a conflict between product requirements?
o: A usability requirement that matches a portability requirement
A capacity requirement that equals a space requirement
A performance requirement contradicted by reliability and security requirements that use processor capacity for dynamic system checking
A safety requirement that reinforces a security requirement
questions.e: Product requirements often conflict; for example, a required level of performance may be contradicted by reliability and security requirements that consume processor capacity to carry out dynamic system checking.

questions.q: The process of arriving at a trade-off between conflicting product requirements depends on which set of factors?
o: The importance attached to the requirement, the consequence of change on other requirements, and the wider business goals
The programming language, compiler and platform
The available CASE tools and management reports
The number of stakeholders and the project budget
questions.e: Resolving conflicts among product requirements is a trade-off that depends on the level of importance attached to the requirement, the consequence of the change on other requirements, and the wider business goals.

questions.q: What are process requirements?
o: Constraints placed upon the development process of the system
Requirements derived from the laws of physics
Desired characteristics that the executing system must possess
Requirements about the quality attributes of the delivered product
questions.e: Process requirements are constraints placed upon the development process of the system, such as development standards, CASE tools, and management reports.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a process requirement?
o: The system shall have an availability of 99%
The system shall be developed for PC and Macintosh platforms
The development process must be conformant with ISO 9000 standards
The system must encrypt communications using RSA
questions.e: Requiring the development process to be explicitly defined and conformant with ISO 9000 standards is a process requirement, constraining how the system is developed rather than the product itself.

questions.q: In the process-requirement example concerning management reports, how often must reports setting out the effort expended on each identified system component be produced?
o: Every month
Every week
Every two weeks
Every two months
questions.e: The process-requirement example states that management reports on the effort expended on each identified system component must be produced every two weeks.

questions.q: Where do external requirements come from, and to what may they apply?
o: Only to hardware, derived from the operating system
Only to the process, derived from CASE tools
Both product and process, derived from the environment in which the system is developed
Only to the product, derived from the source code
questions.e: External requirements may be placed on both the product and the process and are derived from the environment in which the system is developed.

questions.q: Which of the following is cited as a basis for external requirements?
o: The frequency of management reports
Health and safety or data protection regulations
The processor capacity used for dynamic checking
The chosen compiler's code density
questions.e: External requirements are based on factors such as application domain information, organisational considerations, the need to work with other systems, health and safety or data protection regulations, and even basic natural laws such as the laws of physics.

questions.q: Which of the following is identified as a reason why non-functional requirements are difficult to express?
o: Certain constraints relate to a design solution that is unknown at the requirements stage
They are independent of all functional requirements
They are always fully quantifiable at the requirements stage
They never conflict with one another
questions.e: NFRs are difficult to express because certain constraints relate to a design solution unknown at the requirements stage, some are highly subjective, they tend to relate to functional requirements, and they tend to conflict and contradict.

questions.q: Stakeholder 'concerns' are described as typically being of what nature?
o: Purely financial
Strictly hardware-related
Functional
Non-functional
questions.e: Stakeholders normally have a number of concerns, and these concerns are typically non-functional; vaguely defined user concerns may be related to NFRs.

questions.q: In the mapping of user concerns to non-functional requirements, the concern 'Unauthorized Access' corresponds to which NFR?
o: Security
Reliability
Efficiency
Usability
questions.e: Under the user need 'Function', the concern of unauthorized access maps to the non-functional requirement Security, while ease of use maps to Usability and likelihood of failure maps to Reliability.

questions.q: In the mapping of user concerns to NFRs, the user concern 'Resource Utilisation' under the 'Performance' need corresponds to which non-functional requirement?
o: Efficiency
Verifiability
Interoperability
Maintainability
questions.e: Under the user need 'Performance', resource utilisation maps to Efficiency, performance verification maps to Verifiability, and ease of interfacing maps to Interoperability.

questions.q: In the mapping of user concerns to NFRs under the 'Change' need, which concern-to-NFR pairing is correct?
o: Ease of repair maps to Flexibility
Ease of transport maps to Maintainability
Ease of change maps to Flexibility
Ease of expanding capacity maps to Portability
questions.e: Under the 'Change' need, ease of repair maps to Maintainability, ease of change maps to Flexibility, ease of transport maps to Portability, and ease of expanding/upgrading capacity maps to Expandability.

questions.q: The user concern 'Ease of transport' under the 'Change' need corresponds to which non-functional requirement?
o: Maintainability
Flexibility
Expandability
Portability
questions.e: Ease of transport maps to Portability, distinguishing it from ease of repair (Maintainability), ease of change (Flexibility), and ease of expanding capacity (Expandability).

questions.q: Which statement is drawn as a conclusion about non-functional requirements?
o: NFRs are difficult to elicit and express, yet very important for a good-quality system, and conflicts need trade-off analysis
NFRs are easy to elicit and always unambiguous
NFRs are less important than functional requirements
NFRs never conflict and require no trade-offs
questions.e: The concluding points are that NFRs are difficult to elicit and express, are very important for developing a good-quality system, and require resolving conflicts through some trade-off analysis.

questions.q: Requirements analysis is the activity of analysing requirements for problems. Which of the following is NOT one of the categories of problematic requirements identified during this analysis?
o: Conflicting
Duplicated
Verifiable
Confusing
questions.e: Problematic requirements are those that are confusing, extraneous, duplicated, conflicting, or missing. 'Verifiable' is a desirable quality of a good requirement, not a category of problem, making it the exception.

questions.q: What best describes 'requirements agreement' as distinct from requirements analysis?
o: The activity of analysing requirements for problems such as duplication
The process of reconciling differences in the same requirement derived from different sources
The reverse engineering of requirements from an existing system
The mathematical validation of a formal specification
questions.e: Requirements agreement is defined as the process of reconciling differences in the same requirement derived from different sources, often using informal artefacts such as use cases, storyboards, and prototypes. Analysing requirements for problems is a separate activity (requirements analysis).

questions.q: In the classification of requirements specification types, which category do UML and SysML fall into?
o: Behavioural
Informal
Formal
Semiformal
questions.e: UML and SysML (System Modelling Language) are generally considered semiformal modelling techniques because, while appearing informal, they have at least a partial formal basis. Formal techniques have a rigorous mathematical basis; informal ones include natural language and flowcharts.

questions.q: Which statement about informal representation techniques is correct?
o: They include natural language, flowcharts, and ad hoc diagrams, and all SRS documents contain informal elements
They are avoided entirely in the most formal specification documents
They have a partial formal basis, unlike semiformal techniques
They can be completely rewritten into a rigorous mathematical notation
questions.e: Informal techniques include natural language, flowcharts, and ad hoc diagrams, and all SRS documents have informal elements. They cannot be completely rewritten into rigorous mathematical notation, and even the most formal specifications must use natural language to introduce formal elements.

questions.q: In a cited industry study, what percentage of respondents reported that requirements were expressed using informal methods (natural language)?
questions.e: The study reported that 60% of industry respondents expressed requirements using informal methods, specifically natural language, indicating the dominance of informal notation in practice.

questions.q: The standard ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 was released in 2011 by three international standardization bodies. What is the standard's complete name?
o: Systems and Software Engineering—Life Cycle Processes—Requirements Engineering
Requirements Engineering for Software and Systems
Software Requirements Specifications and Design
Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications
questions.e: The complete name of ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 (2011) is 'Systems and Software Engineering—Life Cycle Processes—Requirements Engineering'. It was jointly released by ISO, IEC, and IEEE as a harmonization of several standards.

questions.q: Which three international bodies jointly released Standard 29148 in 2011?
o: ISO, IEC, and IEEE
ISO, ANSI, and IEEE
ISO, IEC, and NASA
PMI, IEC, and IEEE
questions.e: Standard 29148 was jointly released by the International Standards Organization (ISO), the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), and the Institute for Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), harmonizing several different standards.

questions.q: In the Standard 29148 specification document structure, under which top-level section do 'External interfaces', 'Functions', 'Usability requirements', and 'Performance requirements' appear?
o: References
Specific requirements
Introduction
Appendices
questions.e: In the 29148 structure, External interfaces, Functions, Usability requirements, Performance requirements, Logical database requirements, Design constraints, Software system attributes, and Supporting information are all subsections of Section 3, 'Specific requirements'.

questions.q: In the Standard 29148 document outline, where do 'Assumptions and dependencies' and 'Acronyms and abbreviations' appear?
o: In the Verification section
In the Introduction section
In the References section
In the Appendices
questions.e: In the 29148 outline, the Appendices (Section 5) contain 5.1 Assumptions and dependencies and 5.2 Acronyms and abbreviations. Verification (Section 4) runs parallel to the subsections in Section 3.

questions.q: Within the Introduction section of the 29148 document structure, which items are grouped under the 'Product overview' subsection?
o: Product perspective, Product functions, User characteristics, and Limitations
External interfaces, Functions, and Usability requirements
Purpose, Scope, and Definitions
References and Supporting information
questions.e: Under Introduction, the Product overview subsection contains Product perspective, Product functions, User characteristics, and Limitations. Purpose, Scope, and Definitions are separate subsections of the Introduction, not part of Product overview.

questions.q: Why is usability described as an especially important class of requirements, and how can such requirements best be discovered?
o: Because it is a static performance measure; discovered by counting simultaneous users
Because it is easiest to specify formally; discovered through mathematical modelling
Because it defines database integrity constraints; discovered from data retention rules
Because in terms of customer satisfaction it is often the most important class; prototyping can help discover them
questions.e: Usability is often the most important class of requirements for customer satisfaction, yet these requirements are hard to discover in novel systems or new features. Prototyping can be helpful in discovering them.

questions.q: How are performance requirements characterized?
o: Static and dynamic requirements placed on the software or on human interaction with the software as a whole
Requirements derived from applicable laws, standards, or regulations
Requirements about data entities and their relationships
Only static constraints placed on the software alone
questions.e: Performance requirements are static and dynamic requirements placed on the software or on human interaction with the software as a whole, typically including numbers of simultaneous users, transactions, and data processed within time periods under normal and peak workloads.

questions.q: Which of the following is identified as a type of logical database requirement?
o: Screen formats/organization
Integrity constraints
Standards compliance
Number of simultaneous users
questions.e: Logical database requirements cover types of information used by various functions, including frequency of use, accessing capabilities, data entities and their relationships, integrity constraints, and data retention requirements. Screen formats belong to external interface requirements.

questions.q: Software or system attributes such as reliability, availability, security, maintainability, and portability are often collectively termed by what nickname?
o: abilities constraints
ilities (an 'ility')
ities
ances
questions.e: Software or system attributes such as reliability, availability, security, maintainability, and portability are often termed an 'ility'. Other attributes like safety and timeliness are also considered ilities.

questions.q: IEEE 29148 provides several organizational options for functional requirements. Which option is described as 'describing what the system provides to the user'?
o: System mode
User class
Stimulus
Feature
questions.e: Among the organizational options (system mode, user class, object, feature, stimulus, functional hierarchy), organization by 'Feature' describes what the system provides to the user. Functional hierarchy uses top-down decomposition of tasks.

questions.q: In the table contrasting structured and object-oriented approaches, how are data and control specifications handled in the structured approach versus the object-oriented approach?
o: Encapsulated within objects vs. separated through internal decomposition
Separated through internal decomposition vs. encapsulated within objects
Behavioral description vs. functional description
Inheritance relationship vs. hierarchical structure
questions.e: In the structured approach, data and control specifications are separated through internal decomposition; in the object-oriented approach they are encapsulated within objects. Structured also uses hierarchical structure and functional description, whereas object-oriented uses inheritance and behavioral description.

questions.q: Under what circumstance is the system requirements specification (SRS) considered a legally enforceable contract under civil contract law?
o: When there is a customer–vendor relationship between the sponsor and the builders of the system
Only when the SRS follows the IEEE 29148 format
Whenever the SRS uses natural language
When the SRS is reviewed by non-stakeholders
questions.e: The SRS is a contract enforceable under civil contract law (or criminal law in cases of fraud or negligence) specifically where a customer–vendor relationship exists between the sponsor and the builders of the system.

questions.q: The standard form for writing a requirement is given as '[Identifier] The [noun phrase] shall (not) [verb phrase]'. What role does the [Identifier] play?
o: It describes the main subject of the requirement
It indicates the required or prohibited behaviour
It helps in requirement identification for ease of reference, usually with hierarchical numbering
It indicates the actions of the requirement
questions.e: The [Identifier] helps in requirement identification for ease of reference, usually with hierarchical numbering. The noun phrase describes the main subject, 'shall/shall not' indicates required or prohibited behaviour, and the verb phrase indicates the actions.

questions.q: The measurable requirement 'The system shall reject untagged baggage within 5 seconds of identification' extends the standard requirement form by adding which element?
o: A noun phrase
An imperative phrase
An identifier phrase
A constraint phrase
questions.e: The measurable requirements form enriches the standard form to '[identifier] The [noun phrase] shall (not) [verb phrase] [constraint phrase]'. The clause 'within 5 seconds of identification' is the constraint phrase that places a measurable constraint on performance.

questions.q: In the table of imperative words, which imperative is described as being used 'to dictate the provision of a functional capability'?
o: Responsible for
Will
Shall
Must
questions.e: 'Shall' is used to dictate the provision of a functional capability. By contrast, 'Must' establishes performance requirements or constraints, and 'Will' cites things the operational or development environment are to provide.

questions.q: According to the imperatives table, what is the most common use of the imperative 'Will'?
o: To cite things that the operational or development environment are to provide to the capability being specified
To dictate the provision of a functional capability
To include standards by reference as an addition to the requirements
To establish performance requirements or constraints
questions.e: 'Will' is most commonly used to cite things that the operational or development environment are to provide to the capability being specified. 'Shall' dictates a functional capability, while 'Are applicable' includes standards by reference.

questions.q: Regarding the use of 'shall' versus 'shall not', which form does IEEE 29148 recommend?
o: The negative 'shall not' form, because it is clearer
Either form equally, with no preference
Weak imperatives such as 'should' for mandatory requirements
The positive 'shall' form is generally preferred over the negative 'shall not' form
questions.e: It is generally preferred to use the positive 'shall' form rather than the negative 'shall not' form, as recommended by IEEE 29148, though 'shall not' is sometimes desirable to write requirements more clearly.

questions.q: Good practice recommends using 'shall' for mandatory requirements and omitting weak imperatives for optional ones. Which word is cited as the weak imperative used for optional or desirable requirements?
o: Responsible for
Will
Must
Should
questions.e: It is good practice to use 'shall' as the imperative for mandatory requirements and to omit weak imperatives such as 'should' for optional requirements; 'should' is recommended specifically for desirable (optional) requirements.

questions.q: When avoiding imprecision, the vague requirement 'The number of pieces of baggage lost by the system shall be minimal' is improved to which precise form?
o: ...shall be minimized during peak workload
...shall be less than 0.001% of pieces entered
...shall be as low as reasonably possible
...shall be under 5 pieces per day
questions.e: The improved, precise form replaces the vague modifier 'minimal' with a measurable quantity: 'shall be less than 0.001% of pieces entered'. Vague modifiers must be replaced with measurements.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the 'hedging words' to avoid in requirements?
o: Shall
Interface
Probably
Reject
questions.e: The hedging words to avoid include Likely, Almost, Probably, Maybe, and Might be. These introduce uncertainty and should be eliminated from precise requirements.

questions.q: How is a behavioural specification distinguished from a standard SRS?
o: It is generated by reverse engineering an existing system and represents the engineers' best understanding of what users intended, based on inference
It represents the users' best understanding of what the system should do
It is always more complete than a requirements specification
It is a formal mathematical specification with no informal elements
questions.e: A behavioural specification is generated by reverse engineering an existing system whose requirements are missing, incomplete, out of date, or incorrect. It represents the engineers' best understanding of user intent, is based on inference, and can be expected to be even less complete than a requirements specification. The SRS, by contrast, represents the users' best understanding of what the system should do.

questions.q: Which artefact is listed as a source that may be used to derive a behavioural specification?
o: Bug reports and support requests
Text highlighting rules
The imperative words table
Cyclomatic complexity metrics
questions.e: Artefacts used to derive a behavioural specification include any existing requirements specification (even if out of date), user manuals and help information, release notes, bug reports and support requests, application forums, and relevant versions of the software.

questions.q: In the analysis of requirements text structure, what does a 'pyramid' shape indicate about an SRS document?
o: An inconsistent level of detail representation
A well-organized document with a consistent level of detail, with few statements at level 1 and increasingly more at each lower level
A large amount of introductory and administrative information
That the document was generated by reverse engineering
questions.e: A pyramid shape indicates a well-organized SRS with a consistent level of detail: few numbered statements at level 1 and increasingly more at each lower level. An hourglass indicates much introductory/administrative content, and a diamond indicates inconsistent detail.

questions.q: A requirements document whose statement counts per level form a pyramid followed by decreasing counts at lower levels produces which shape, and what does it indicate?
o: Pyramid shape, indicating a consistent level of detail
Rectangular shape, indicating uniform detail
Diamond shape, indicating an inconsistent level of detail representation
Hourglass shape, indicating much administrative information
questions.e: A diamond-shaped document (a pyramid followed by decreasing statement counts at lower levels) indicates an inconsistent level of detail representation. The hourglass shape instead signals a large amount of introductory and administrative information.

questions.q: In the requirements numbering scheme, what level of abstraction is expected for first-level requirements numbered 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, and so forth?
o: The most detailed, low-level requirements
Third-level implementation requirements
Very high-level (abstract) requirements
Subordinate requirements at a lower level of detail
questions.e: First-level requirements numbered 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 are expected to be very high-level (abstract). Second-level requirements (1.1, 1.2, ...) are subordinate at a lower level of detail, and third-level (1.1.1, 1.1.2) are even more detailed.

questions.q: Among the best practices for writing requirements, why should conjunctions such as 'and', 'or', and 'but' be avoided in a single statement?
o: Because they cannot be verified
Because they are technical language
Because they can lead to multiple requirements in a single statement
Because they are hedging words
questions.e: Conjunctions such as 'and', 'or', and 'but' should be avoided because they can lead to multiple requirements being packed into a single statement. Separately avoided items include rambling phrases, hedging clauses, speculative terms, and vague terms like 'user friendly'.

questions.q: The unverifiable requirement 'The system shall be modular' is given an improved, verifiable form. What is that improved form?
o: 95% of the transactions shall be processed in less than 1s
Response times for all level one actions will be less than 100ms
The cyclomatic complexity of each module shall be in the range of 10 to 40
Mean time before first failure shall be 100 hours of continuous operation
questions.e: 'The system shall be modular' is improved to the verifiable form 'The cyclomatic complexity of each module shall be in the range of 10 to 40'. The other options are the improved forms of the reliability, speed, and error-rate requirements respectively.

questions.q: In the worked measurable-requirement example for a baggage scanner, the planned value and lowest acceptable value are defined relative to a reference value (the average time of competing products). What are the planned and lowest acceptable values?
o: Planned value 30% less, lowest acceptable value 50% less than reference
Planned value 10 pieces per minute, lowest acceptable value 5 pieces per minute
Planned value equal to reference, lowest acceptable value 30% less
Planned value 50% less, lowest acceptable value 30% less than reference
questions.e: For the scanner attribute (average scan time), the planned value is 50% less than the reference value and the lowest acceptable value is 30% less than the reference value, where the reference value is the average time needed by competing or similar products.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of system modelling in the analysis and design process?
o: To eliminate the need for any requirements documentation
To introduce a degree of formality into the way systems are defined
