To guarantee a single correct solution for every problem
To replace communication between stakeholders with automated tools
questions.e: System modelling supports the analysis and design process by introducing a degree of formality into the way systems are defined. It is described as the most creative aspect, with no single 'right' solution.

questions.q: Which statement best characterizes a good system model?
o: One that contains the maximum possible detail
One that never changes once created
One that is easily communicated
One that is mathematically provable to be correct
questions.e: A good model is one which is easily communicated. Models have no single 'right' solution and evolve over time.

questions.q: Which of the following is stated as a benefit of modelling?
o: It removes the need for validation of the system design
It prevents the system from being viewed from multiple perspectives
It replaces the need for standard notations between organizations
It encourages the use of a precisely defined vocabulary consistent across the system
questions.e: Benefits of modelling include encouraging a precisely defined vocabulary consistent across the system, allowing visualization in diagrams, and considering multiple interacting aspects and views.

questions.q: How does modelling allow validation of some aspects of the system design?
o: Through manual code inspection only
Through user surveys
Through animation
Through hardware testing
questions.e: Modelling allows validation of some aspects of the system design through animation, and supports progressive refinement toward detailed design, permitting test case and code generation.

questions.q: Data flow diagrams (DFDs) are described as the basis of what?
o: Agile development frameworks
Object-oriented programming languages
Database normalization techniques
Most traditional modelling methods
questions.e: Data flow diagrams (DFDs) are the basis of most traditional modelling methods and can be used to represent any type of system.

questions.q: In DFD notation, how are data transformations (processes) represented?
o: Horizontal parallel lines
Rectangles
Labelled arrows
Circles or 'bubbles'
questions.e: In DFDs, data transformations are shown as circles or 'bubbles'. Data flows are labelled arrows, data stores are horizontal parallel lines, and external entities are rectangles.

questions.q: In DFD notation, external entities and data stores are represented, respectively, by which symbols?
o: Labelled arrows and circles
Rectangles and horizontal parallel lines
Circles and rectangles
Horizontal parallel lines and rectangles
questions.e: External entities are shown as rectangles and data stores as horizontal parallel lines in DFDs, while data flows are labelled arrows and transformations are circles/bubbles.

questions.q: When using DFD notation, what must the diagrams be supported by?
o: A UML class diagram for each process
A cost-benefit analysis
Textual descriptions of each process, data store and flow
A relational database schema
questions.e: When using DFD notation, diagrams must be supported by textual descriptions of each process, data store and flow.

questions.q: What does the context diagram represent in a DFD?
o: The most detailed decomposition of every process
The internal state transitions of a single process
The top-level diagram showing the external systems interacting with the proposed system
A listing of all data stores in alphabetical order
questions.e: The context diagram is the top-level diagram of a DFD and shows the external systems interacting with the proposed system.

questions.q: How can the functional hierarchy in a set of data flow diagrams be used?
o: Only to document the user interface
To measure the performance of the running system
As a framework for deriving and structuring system requirements
To replace entity-relationship modelling entirely
questions.e: The functional hierarchy in a set of data flow diagrams can be used as a framework for deriving and structuring system requirements.

questions.q: In DFDs, how can system transactions be marked to identify information flow paths and the functions used?
o: With shaded rectangles
With thick arrows
With dashed circles
With numbered data stores
questions.e: System transactions can be marked with the help of thick arrows identifying the information flow path and the functions used.

questions.q: Who originally proposed Entity-Relationship modeling, and in what year?
o: Ivar Jacobson in 1992
Peter Chen in 1976
Edgar Codd in 1970
Grady Booch in 1991
questions.e: Entity-Relationship modeling was originally proposed by Peter Chen in 1976.

questions.q: In Entity-Relationship modeling, what do the related entity types of a relationship also get called?
o: Multiplicities
Instances
Attributes
Roles
questions.e: In ERM a relationship represents relationship instances holding between pairs of entity instances, and the related entity types are also called roles.

questions.q: In Entity-Relationship modeling, what does multiplicity information indicate?
o: The number of attributes an entity may have
How many instances of the 'other' side may be related to a given instance of 'this' side
The data type of each attribute
The order in which entities were created
questions.e: Multiplicity information indicates how many instances of the 'other' side may be related to a given instance of 'this' side.

questions.q: In ERM, an attribute is identified by which of the following?
o: A relationship instance
An inheritance path
A role and a multiplicity
A name and its type
questions.e: In ERM, each attribute is identified by a name and its type, where the type is usually a simple data type such as integer or character string.

questions.q: Which notation is noted as having more powerful multiplicity notation than other ERM notations?
o: UML Class Diagram notation
Crow's foot notation
'Normal' ERM notation
Data Flow Diagram notation
questions.e: Among ERM notations ('normal', Crow's foot, and UML Class Diagram), the notation for multiplicities in UML is described as more powerful than the others; the concepts, however, are the same across notations.

questions.q: Object-oriented modeling is essentially ERM with additional concepts. What is an Entity called in OOM?
o: A role
A data store
A class
A transformation
questions.e: Object-oriented modeling is essentially ERM with certain additional concepts, and an Entity is called a Class.

questions.q: In object-oriented modeling, what does it mean when entity B inherits all properties defined for entity A?
o: B is a specialization (refinement) of A
B and A are unrelated instances
A is composed of B
A calls methods on B
questions.e: Inheritance is the idea that entity B inherits all properties defined for entity A, meaning B is a specialization (also called a refinement or extension) of A.

questions.q: In OOM, which additional concept means certain internal attributes are not directly accessible from outside the entity instance?
o: Multiplicity
Inheritance
Composite structure
Information hiding
questions.e: OOM introduces internal state and methods for interacting with it; an important issue is information hiding, in which certain internal attributes are not directly accessible from outside the entity instance.

questions.q: In OOM, which refined relationship subtype shows that one entity is part of another (composed) entity?
o: Composite structure
Inheritance
Calling relationship
Multiplicity constraint
questions.e: Composite structure is a subtype of Relationship (with special notation) used to show that one entity is part of another (composed) entity, whereas a calling relationship lets an instance access attributes and call methods on a related instance.

questions.q: Which is stated as a disadvantage of object-oriented modeling?
o: Difficulty of modeling two-way communication, since an interface defines only one direction
It only works for database systems
It requires no notation at all
It cannot represent inheritance
questions.e: A disadvantage of OOM is difficulty modeling two-way communication because an interface defines only one direction; event-based systems often need two-way communication. Encapsulation via information hiding is also often unsuitable for modeling the problem domain during requirements engineering.

questions.q: Which modelling approach is credited with unifying many of the earlier object-oriented notations?
o: UML
Data Flow Diagrams
Entity-Relationship modeling
Crow's foot notation
questions.e: Among the proposed OO analysis approaches (Shlaer & Mellor, Coad & Yourdon, Rumbaugh, Jacobson, RUP, and others), UML unifies many of these notations.

questions.q: How many main steps are in the described methodology for Object-Oriented Analysis (OOA)?
o: Four
Five
Three
Six
questions.e: The methodology for Object-Oriented Analysis has five main steps: identify core classes, model relationships between classes, define attributes, determine operations, and define messages passed between objects.

questions.q: What is the first step in the described Object-Oriented Analysis methodology?
o: Model relationships between classes
Identify core classes within the problem domain
Define the messages passed between objects
Determine relevant operations for each class
questions.e: The first main step of the OOA methodology is to identify core classes within the problem domain; modelling relationships, defining attributes, determining operations, and defining messages follow.

questions.q: In the library OOA example, from which three primary groups are library users drawn?
o: Published, recorded, and registered users
Administrators, assistants, and members
Borrowers, cataloguers, and browsers
Students, members of staff, and external users
questions.e: In the library example, library users are drawn from three primary groups: students, members of staff, and external users.

questions.q: In the library example, which extra registration information is required for a student versus an external user?
o: Staff number, versus degree programme
Library number, versus account
Employer details, versus staff number
Degree programme and admission number, versus employer details
questions.e: All users register with name, library number, address, and account; students additionally require degree programme and admission number, external users require employer details, and staff require a staff number.

questions.q: In Step 4 of the library OOA example, which operations are described as implicit and need not be shown explicitly in the model?
o: CRUD operations and getters/setters
Inheritance and composition operations
Message-passing and interaction operations
Registration and cataloguing operations
questions.e: Certain operations are implicit from the object structure, namely CRUD (create, read, update, delete) operations and getters/setters for accessing and modifying attribute values; these are assumed and need not be shown explicitly.

questions.q: In Step 4 of the library example, what is one way of identifying object operations?
o: By listing all external entities
By drawing the context diagram
By modeling the messages that may be passed between the objects
By counting the attributes of each class
questions.e: One way of identifying operations is by modeling the messages that may be passed between the objects; required messages are found for each scenario and then the union of all messages is taken.

questions.q: What caution is raised about most OOA approaches?
o: They cannot model inheritance
They actually address detail-level design and assume a pre-existing requirements document
They only work for library systems
They require no class diagrams
questions.e: A caution is that most OOA approaches are 'not really analysis' but actually address detail-level design and assume a pre-existing requirements document; class diagrams can still be used for analysis, especially for describing domain concepts.

questions.q: Which technique is said to supplement OOA by filling in some gaps?
o: Functional decomposition
Crow's foot notation
Use case analysis
Data flow analysis
questions.e: Use case analysis supplements OOA, filling in some gaps, since OOA has composition and decomposition problems where related requirements cannot all be assigned to a single class and one scenario may affect several classes at once.

questions.q: What does the goal modelling paradigm encourage as the mechanism by which the 'form' of an artefact meeting an originally stated goal is defined?
o: The development of goal networks through successive refinement of goals
The immediate translation of goals into program code
The ranking of goals purely by financial cost
The elimination of ambiguous goals from the requirements set
questions.e: The paradigm encourages the development of goal networks whereby successive refinement of goals leads to the definition of the 'form' of the artefact that meets the originally stated goal. The other options are not the described mechanism.

questions.q: Work in the area of goals is described as spanning which set of disciplines?
o: Business administration, social science and computer science
Law, medicine and architecture
Psychology, linguistics and economics
Mathematics, physics and engineering
questions.e: Goal-related work spans multiple disciplines, specifically business administration, social science, and computer science. The other groupings are not the ones cited.

questions.q: Which three goal-oriented approaches are named as computer-science approaches that explicitly represent goals and build an enterprise model around them?
o: UML, BPMN and ArchiMate
SADT, IDEF0 and DFD
KAOS, F3 and EKD
SSADM, Yourdon and Jackson
questions.e: The named goal-oriented approaches in computer science are KAOS, F3, and EKD. The other listed methods are not identified as goal-oriented approaches here.

questions.q: In their majority, what kind of goal structure do goal modelling environments use to store and organise goals?
o: Binary decision trees only
Relational database tables
Flat unordered lists
A graph-like structure, usually AND/OR graphs
questions.e: Goal modelling environments in their majority use a graph-like goal structure, usually AND/OR graphs, to store and organise goals. The other structures are not described.

questions.q: The F3 approach to requirements engineering takes its name from which phrase?
o: From Fuzzy to Formal
Framework for Functional Forms
Formal to Functional
Fast, Flexible, Formal
questions.e: F3 stands for 'From Fuzzy to Formal', its view on requirements engineering. The other expansions are not correct.

questions.q: A goal is used for expressing intentionality and may be expressed as measurable sets of which of the following?
o: Actors, roles and resources
States, visions, aims or directions
Costs, risks and schedules
Classes, objects and attributes
questions.e: A goal expresses intentionality and may be expressed as measurable sets of states, visions, aims or directions. The other groupings are not how a goal is characterised.

questions.q: How is the basic structure of a goal expressed?
o: By a subject, verb and object only
By a verb plus n parameters
By a numeric priority plus a description
By a noun plus an adjective
questions.e: A goal is expressed by a verb plus n parameters. For instance 'Reduce power failures by 10% for the 5 forthcoming years' has a verb plus object, quantity and time parameters.

questions.q: In the goal 'Reduce power failures by 10% for the 5 forthcoming years', which parameter type does the element '5 forthcoming years' represent?
o: Object
Time
Quantity
Manner
questions.e: 'Reduce' is the verb, 'power failures' the object, 'by 10%' the quantity, and 'for the 5 forthcoming years' is the time parameter. The other labels apply to different parts of the goal.

questions.q: In the goal 'Estimate load needs efficiently', what kind of parameter is 'efficiently'?
o: An object parameter
A manner parameter
A time parameter
A quantity parameter
questions.e: In 'Estimate (verb) load needs (object) efficiently (manner)', the word 'efficiently' is the manner parameter. It is not a time, quantity or object parameter.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the two matrix notations named for goal modelling?
o: Traceability Matrix
Responsibility Assignment Matrix
Risk Impact Matrix
Issue Goal Matrix
questions.e: The two matrix notations named for goal modelling are the Issue Goal Matrix and the Goal Correlation Matrix. The other matrices are not listed among the goal-modelling notations.

questions.q: Among the implications of goal modelling, which pair is given as contributing to the complexity of the goal model?
o: Verb parameters and operationalisation links
Different stakeholder contexts and voting procedures
Multiple goal refinement alternatives and conflicting goals
Heterogeneity of sources and lack of techniques
questions.e: The complexity of the goal model is attributed to multiple goal refinement alternatives and conflicting goals. Heterogeneity of information sources and lack of techniques are listed as separate implications rather than as the source of model complexity.

questions.q: What kind of approach is recommended for eliciting goals from stakeholders who often have opposing goals?
o: A single-expert interview approach
A co-operative, discussant approach
An automated approach with no human input
A strictly hierarchical top-down mandate
questions.e: Because stakeholders have different, often opposing goals, a co-operative, discussant approach is needed, in which topics can be loosely defined, goals categorised and prioritised through voting, and dominant participants do not adversely affect the outcome.

questions.q: Which of the following is named as one of the useful tools supporting cooperation, deliberation and agreement in goal elicitation?
o: Entity-Relationship Editor
Gantt Chart
Compiler
Electronic Brainstorming
questions.e: The useful tools listed are Categoriser, Electronic Brainstorming, Group Outliner, Topic Commenter and Vote. The other options are not among these tools.

questions.q: In 'bottom up' goal modelling using role models, what relationship do the goals presented in the 'body' of each role have to the business goal?
o: They contradict the business goal
They replace the business goal entirely
They are unrelated to the business process
They support the achievement of the business goal realised by the business process
questions.e: The goals presented in the body of each role support the achievement of the business goal realised by the business process. Role goals are mainly operational goals expressed in terms of business objects and activities.

questions.q: What is the stated objective of actor modelling?
o: To calculate the cost of achieving each goal
To describe co-operation between different organisational actors such as human individuals, IT systems and workgroups
To generate source code from goal graphs
To store goals in relational tables
questions.e: Actor modelling aims to describe co-operation between different organisational actors, for example human individuals, IT systems and workgroups. The other options are not its objective.

questions.q: How is a goal defined in the context of organisational actors?
o: A mandatory activity assigned to an IT system
A measurable financial target set annually
A desired condition potentially attained at the end of an action or process
A conflict between two stakeholders
questions.e: A goal is defined as a desired condition potentially attained at the end of an action or process. Organisational actors have goals which they discharge through their roles.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between roles and the people who perform them?
o: Roles are instances and actors are types
A role can only ever be acted by one specific actor for its whole lifetime
Roles are types, role instances are acted, and a role exists independently of who is acting it
A role and its actor are always the same entity
questions.e: Roles are types, role instances are acted, and a role exists independently of who is acting it at any one time. This is distinct from actors, which are instances of actor types.

questions.q: Given that the Prime Ministers of Pakistan, Australia and Canada are cited as instances of the same actor type, and that one person can act as Prime Minister and Member of Senate, what two principles are being illustrated?
o: An actor is an instance of an actor type, and an actor may play many roles
An actor is a type, and a role may be played by many actors simultaneously
An actor and a role are identical concepts
A role is an instance of a goal, and a goal may have many actors
questions.e: The examples illustrate that an actor is an instance of an actor type (e.g. Prime Minister) and that an actor may play many roles (Prime Minister, Member of Senate, etc.).

questions.q: Which of the following is named as an actor modelling approach?
o: KAOS
EKD
F3
RADs (Role Activity Diagrams)
questions.e: The actor modelling approaches named are i*, Actor Role Modelling, RADs (Role Activity Diagrams) and Role Interaction Nets. KAOS, F3 and EKD are named as goal-oriented approaches rather than actor modelling approaches.

questions.q: In the semantics of the actor-role diagram, an Actor is best described as which of the following?
o: A collection of responsibilities
A desired condition attained at the end of a process
A dependency between two roles
An organisational entity to which the fulfilment of a role is assigned
questions.e: A Role represents a collection of responsibilities, while an Actor represents an organisational entity to which the fulfilment of a role is assigned. A goal is the desired condition, and dependencies link roles.

questions.q: How many types of dependency exist between roles in the actor-role diagram, and what are they?
o: Two: Goal and Resource
Four: Authorisation, Goal, Co-ordination and Resource
Five: Authorisation, Goal, Coordination, Resource and Trust
Three: Goal, Resource and Coordination
questions.e: There exist four types of dependency between roles: Authorisation (A), Goal (G), Co-ordination (C) and Resource (R). The other counts and combinations are incorrect.

questions.q: According to the conclusion, goal modelling helps identify organizational goals and how they are realized in which two models?
o: The AS-IS model (existing environment) and the TO-BE model (future)
The static model and the dynamic model
The AND model and the OR model
The logical model and the physical model
questions.e: Goal modelling helps identify how goals are realized in the existing environment (AS-IS model) or how they must be achieved in the future (TO-BE model). It also helps identify conflicting requirements based on conflicting goals.

questions.q: Requirements management is best described as a systematic approach to eliciting, organizing, and documenting the requirements of a system, and additionally to which of the following?
o: Transferring ownership of all requirements to the supplier organization
Guaranteeing that no requirement will ever change once the contract is signed
Establishing and maintaining agreement between the customer and the project team on the changing requirements of the system
Eliminating the need for a defined change control process
questions.e: Requirements management is a systematic approach both to eliciting, organizing, and documenting requirements and to establishing and maintaining agreement between the customer and the project team on the system's changing requirements. It explicitly accommodates change rather than preventing it.

questions.q: Every project is said to be constrained by three related fundamental factors. Which set correctly names all three?
o: Product capability/quality, cost, and time-scale
Planning, monitoring, and change control
Scope, staffing, and stakeholder satisfaction
Elicitation, documentation, and validation
questions.e: The three fundamental constraining factors are product capability/quality, cost, and time-scale. They are related, so any change to one has a consequential change to at least one of the others.

questions.q: It is stated that any change to one of a project's three fundamental factors will have what effect on the others?
o: It has a consequential change to at least one of the others
It leaves the other two factors unaffected
It automatically improves both of the other two factors
It only affects cost, never capability or time-scale
questions.e: Because product capability/quality, cost, and time-scale are related, any change to one of these factors will have a consequential change to at least one of the others.

questions.q: What is given as the main reason why very few people have significant experience of managing requirements?
o: Very few organizations have a defined requirements management process that is followed across the organization
Requirements rarely change, so the skill is seldom needed
Requirements management tools are too expensive for most companies
University programs never teach requirements engineering
questions.e: The scarcity of experience is attributed mainly to the fact that very few organizations have a defined requirements management process that is followed across the organization.

questions.q: Among the identified requirements management problems, which distinction do many people fail to make?
o: Between hardware and software requirements
Between functional and non-functional requirements
Between user/stakeholder requirements and system requirements
Between mandatory and optional requirements
questions.e: A noted problem is that many people do not properly distinguish between user/stakeholder requirements and system requirements, and further often fail to distinguish system requirements from design specifications.

questions.q: The three specific management issues addressed in requirements management are planning, monitoring progress, and which third issue?
o: Recruiting stakeholders
Negotiating the final invoice
Manufacturing the product
Controlling changes (change management)
questions.e: The specific management issues are planning, monitoring progress, and controlling changes, the last of which is change management.

questions.q: An organization that purchases systems and then uses them to provide an operational capability, and is mainly concerned with creating and managing stakeholder requirements, is called what?
o: A subcontracting organization
A supplier organization
A product organization
An acquisition organization
questions.e: Acquisition organizations purchase systems and use them to provide an operational capability; they are mainly concerned with creating and managing stakeholder requirements.

questions.q: Which type of organization receives input requirements and develops system requirements (and subsequently a design that is manufactured) in response to acquisition requests?
o: Acquisition organizations
Supplier organizations
Operations organizations
Product organizations
questions.e: Supplier organizations respond to acquisition requests by receiving input requirements and developing system requirements, and subsequently a design that is manufactured, in response to them.

questions.q: How do product companies primarily obtain their stakeholder requirements, in contrast to acquisition organizations?
o: From government acquisition requests only
From subcontractors executing a contract
From their market place rather than from individuals or operations organizations
From an invitation to tender issued by a supplier
questions.e: Product companies develop and sell products and collect stakeholder requirements from their market place, rather than from individuals or from operations organizations.

questions.q: Three major milestones are said to help define the monitoring of requirements work. Which of the following is one of them?
o: The signing of the final acceptance certificate
The delivery of the manufactured system
The definition of the structure for the requirements specification
The selection of the winning bidder
questions.e: The three monitoring milestones are the definition of the structure for the requirements specification, the definition of the attributes required for each requirement, and the definition of the review process(es) with associated checklists.

questions.q: Whatever stage a project is at, the change control process requires four steps in order. Which sequence is correct?
o: Decide when to implement, record the change, identify the impact, decide whether to accept
Record the suggested change, decide whether to accept, decide when to implement, identify the impact
Record the suggested change, identify the impact, decide whether to accept, decide when to implement
Identify the impact, decide whether to accept, record the change, decide when to implement
questions.e: The change control process steps are: record the suggested change, identify the impact of the suggested change, decide whether to accept the change, and decide when to implement the change.

questions.q: Supplier organizations are considered from which two points of view?
o: Planning and decommissioning
Bidding for work and executing a contract
Specifying and manufacturing
Eliciting and validating
questions.e: Supplier organizations are considered from two points of view: bidding for work and executing a contract. Prior to a contract they must prepare a proposal with estimates of cost and time.

questions.q: If the customer issuing an invitation to tender (ITT) or request for proposal (RFP) is another supplier organization planning to subcontract, the requirements received are most likely to be what?
o: Stakeholder/user requirements
System requirements with imposed design constraints
Operational scenarios only
Marketing requirements gathered from the market place
questions.e: When the customer is an acquisition organization the requirements are likely to be stakeholder/user requirements, but when the customer is another supplier planning to subcontract, the requirements are likely to be system requirements with imposed design constraints.

questions.q: Whatever their nature, input requirements received in a bid need to be clearly identified, unambiguous, consistent, and which of the following?
o: Approved by the manufacturing department
Limited to a single release
Written by the supplier's design team
Free from undue design constraints
questions.e: Input requirements need to be clearly identified, unambiguous, consistent, and free from undue design constraints before a proposal is prepared.

questions.q: When reviewing input requirements and finding a specific problem, which is one of the listed possible options for handling that problem?
o: Postpone the whole bid indefinitely
Refer it directly to the manufacturing line
Delete the requirement without any record
Make an assumption and document it
questions.e: The possible options for each identified problem are to ignore it, to make an assumption and document it, or to decide that it is essential to ask the customer whatever the consequences.

questions.q: Why is measuring progress during creation of a proposal described as vital?
o: Because suppliers are legally required to publish progress reports
Because manufacturing has already begun
Because the customer pays per requirement documented
Because time-scales are usually constrained and the submission date is not negotiable
questions.e: Measuring progress during proposal creation is vital because time-scales are usually constrained and the submission date is not negotiable.

questions.q: During preparation of a proposal, the three potential sources of change identified are the customer, internal, and which third?
o: Suppliers
The manufacturing plant
End users in the field
Regulators
questions.e: The three potential sources of change during proposal preparation are the customer, suppliers, and internal. The probability of change is roughly proportional to the size of the system to be developed.

questions.q: The probability of change during bidding is said to be roughly proportional to what?
o: The number of suppliers involved
The experience of the bid team
The size of the system to be developed
The length of the submission deadline
questions.e: Typically the probability of change is roughly proportional to the size of the system to be developed.

questions.q: To keep bid work consistent, several requirements baselines must be kept up-to-date. Which of the following is one of those baselines?
o: The manufacturing schedule
Assumptions and interpretations made within the bid team
The customer's marketing plan
The final acceptance test results
questions.e: Whatever the source of change, the requirements baselines that must be kept up-to-date are input requirements, requirements placed on suppliers, and assumptions and interpretations made within the bid team.

questions.q: Once a development contract is agreed based on the submitted proposal, what happens to the accepted proposal?
o: It becomes part of the input requirements
It becomes the sole design specification
It is handed to the customer's operations department
It is discarded because the contract supersedes it
questions.e: The development stage commences with an agreed contract based on the proposal as modified during negotiations, and the accepted proposal now becomes part of the input requirements.

questions.q: To record whether each requirement belongs to a single or an incremental release, a release attribute can be added to each requirement. What is a given example of a possible enumeration list of values, and what does its first value stand for?
o: {Low, Medium, High}, where Low stands for optional
{TBD, Release 1, Release 2, Release 3}, where TBD stands for to be decided
{Draft, Final, Archived}, where Draft stands for temporary
{Specify, Develop, Use}, where Specify stands for start
questions.e: A possible enumeration list for a release attribute is {TBD, Release 1, Release 2, Release 3}, where TBD stands for to be decided.

questions.q: How does the extent of customer-driven changes during development compare with that during bidding, and how serious are the consequences?
o: There are no customer changes during development
Customer changes are far less during development, but the consequence of a change is far more serious
Customer changes are identical in both stages with identical consequences
Customer changes are far greater during development, and consequences are trivial
questions.e: The extent of customer changes is likely to be far less during development than during bidding, yet the consequence of a change at the development stage is far more serious. Internal and supplier changes remain just as likely.

questions.q: Changes introduced during development will usually have an impact on which aspects, making the decision to absorb penalties or renegotiate a commercial one?
o: Only the product capability, never cost or schedule
Both the time-scale (schedule) of the development and the cost
Only the requirements traceability links
Only the review checklist criteria
questions.e: Changes during development usually impact both the time-scale (schedule) and the cost, after which it is a commercial decision whether to absorb the penalties or negotiate with the customer and/or suppliers.

questions.q: What is described as the main difference between product organizations and acquisition/supplier organizations?
o: Product organizations never monitor progress
The customer–supplier agreement at the top level of the supply chain is within the overall organization
Product organizations do not use requirements at all
Product organizations only build one product version at a time
questions.e: Product organizations share many characteristics with acquisition and supplier organizations, but the main difference is that the customer–supplier agreement at the top level of the supply chain is within the overall organization, with different departments defining requirements and developing products.

questions.q: When gathering stakeholder requirements for a single product version, rather than always interviewing real stakeholders, what commonly happens?
o: The supplier defines all requirements alone with no roles
Requirements are copied verbatim from a competitor
Stakeholders are replaced by automated tools
People volunteer or are volunteered to act as surrogate stakeholders
questions.e: For a single product version there is still a need to identify stakeholders and user scenarios, but rather than interviewing real stakeholders, people commonly volunteer or are volunteered to act as surrogate stakeholders who adopt a defined stakeholder role.

questions.q: In the context of multiple products, the term 'variant' is used to mean what?
o: Differing in form or details from the main one
A requirement that cannot be traced
A defect found during acceptance trials
A release scheduled for a future date
questions.e: The notion of a variant is used to mean differing in form or details from the main one; for example, user interfaces supporting different natural languages for different countries.

questions.q: From a requirements management viewpoint, how do a variant and the versions of that variant relate to requirements?
o: Versions differ in requirements but variants never do

A variant has requirements common with the core product plus some specific to it, while different versions of a variant may have no different requirements because each version tries to satisfy the same set
Variants share no requirements with the core product
Every version of a variant has a completely different requirement set
questions.e: Each variant shares many requirements with the core product but has some specific requirements that differentiate it from other variants; meanwhile there may be no different requirements for each version of a variant, since each version attempts to satisfy the same set of requirements.

questions.q: When a change proposal is raised against variants that share common requirements, when can the change achieve the status of complete?
o: As soon as the change is recorded
Only when all the variants have reached their individual incorporated state
When the first variant reaches its incorporated state
When the customer signs the contract
questions.e: For shared requirements across variants, planned, deferred and incorporated states are needed for each variant, and the change can only achieve the status of complete when all the variants have reached their individual incorporated state.

questions.q: Barry Boehm distinguished verification from validation using two questions. Which question corresponds to requirements validation?
o: "Am I building the right product?"
"Am I building the product right?"
"Am I testing the product enough?"
"Am I documenting the product correctly?"
questions.e: Boehm framed validation as "Am I building the right product?" (fully understanding customer intent), whereas verification is "Am I building the product right?" (satisfying that intent).

questions.q: In Boehm's distinction, requirements validation is chiefly concerned with which of the following?
o: Satisfying customer intent
Fully understanding customer intent
Collecting inspection defect data
Automating consistency queries
questions.e: Validation involves fully understanding customer intent (building the right product), while verification is about satisfying that intent (building the product right).

questions.q: Requirements validation and verification is described as involving which combination of activities to ensure a system complies with its requirements?
o: Coding, debugging and deployment
Review, analysis and testing
Elicitation, negotiation and prioritisation
Estimation, scheduling and budgeting
questions.e: Requirements V&V involves review, analysis and testing to ensure a system complies with its requirements, and applies to both functional and non-functional requirements.

questions.q: A controller for an electric water heater is specified as: if 70°<temp<100° output 3000 W; if 100°<temp<130° output 2000 W; if 120°<temp<150° output 1000 W; if 150°<temp output 0 W. What problem is illustrated by the overlap between the 100°-130° and 120°-150° ranges?
o: Ambiguity of the term 'watts'
Inconsistency, because overlapping ranges specify conflicting outputs
Incompleteness only
Perfect consistency and completeness
questions.e: For temperatures between 120° and 130° two rules apply (2000 W and 1000 W), so the overlapping ranges make the requirements inconsistent; the set was used to show non-verifiable requirements.

questions.q: Which technique is NOT among the listed requirements V&V techniques?
o: Prototyping
Code refactoring
Animation-based validation
Test case development
questions.e: The V&V techniques listed are inspections & reviews, prototyping, test case development, acceptance criteria, queries on the requirements database, and animation-based validation; code refactoring is not among them.

questions.q: A semistructured meeting where requirements engineers, a supervisor, and peers informally review requirements prior to release to find ambiguities and inconsistencies is best described as a:
o: Acceptance test
Fagan inspection
Database query
Walkthrough
questions.e: A walkthrough (peer/team review) is an informal method involving requirements engineers, a supervisor and peers in a semistructured meeting to identify ambiguities, inconsistencies and testability issues.

questions.q: Which standard's rules can serve as a framework or checklist during a requirements walkthrough?
o: IEEE 830
IEEE 29148
Fagan 1986
ISO 9001
questions.e: The IEEE 29148 rules can be used as a framework or checklist for a walkthrough to help detect errors and improve requirements quality.

questions.q: The formal, highly structured inspection process that provides close procedural control and repeatability is attributed to whom?
o: Awais Majeed
Phillip Laplante
Michael Fagan
Barry Boehm
questions.e: More formal inspection processes such as those described by Fagan (1986) provide close procedural control and repeatability; the process was developed by Michael Fagan at IBM.

questions.q: For which kind of system is inspection said to be especially appropriate?
o: Legacy batch systems
Purely cosmetic user interfaces
Prototype throwaway systems
Safety-critical systems
questions.e: Inspection can be used in many requirements engineering settings but is especially appropriate for safety-critical systems.

questions.q: Fagan inspections explicitly define all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Who can inspect and how the inspection is conducted
The salary paid to each inspector
The data to be collected and follow-up activities
What can be inspected and when
questions.e: Fagan inspections define what can be inspected, when, who can inspect, what preparation is needed, how it is conducted, the data to be collected, and follow-up activities; inspector salary is not among them.

questions.q: Requirements inspection foundations are based on inspections originally carried out for which artifact?
o: Project plans
Source code
Design diagrams
Test documentation
questions.e: The inspection foundation is based on inspections carried out for source code, with the process developed by Michael Fagan at IBM, and it can be applied to any software artefact.

questions.q: Which of the following is an INFORMAL peer review approach rather than a formal one?
o: A formal peer review with a defined process
A Fagan inspection with defect data collection
An inspection
A peer deskcheck
questions.e: Informal approaches include a peer deskcheck, a passaround, and a walkthrough; the best-established formal peer review is the inspection.

questions.q: The best-established type of formal peer review is called a(n):
o: Deskcheck
Walkthrough
Inspection
Passaround
questions.e: Reviews can be informal or formal; the best-established type of formal peer review is called an inspection.

questions.q: Companies inspecting requirements documents have reportedly avoided as much labour as which figure for every hour invested?
o: As much as 10 hours per hour invested
As much as 100 hours per hour invested
As much as 2 hours per hour invested
As much as 5 hours per hour invested
questions.e: Several companies have avoided as much as 10 hours of labour for every hour they invested in inspecting requirements documents and other deliverables, and studies show inspection can outperform code testing.

questions.q: During individual reviewing in the inspection process, which reading mode is NOT listed?
o: Pair-programming based
Free mode
Process based
Checklist based
questions.e: Each inspector reads the requirements document individually using one of three modes: free mode, checklist based, or process based; pair-programming based is not among them.

questions.q: At the defect evaluation review meeting, which defects are kept for follow-up action?
o: Only defects for which there is agreement among participants
Only defects found in safety-critical sections
All defects found by any single inspector
Only defects reported by the supervisor
questions.e: Defects found by each inspector are discussed, and only those for which there is agreement are kept; the aim is to discard false positives before analysing causes and recommending actions.

questions.q: According to the inspection guidelines, an inspection report should:
o: Be specific, informative, factual and constructive
Be written to challenge the authors personally
Contain opinions rather than facts
Be as heavyweight and detailed as possible
questions.e: The WHAT guideline states the inspection report should be specific and informative, contain facts not opinions, be constructive and not offensive to the authors, and have a lightweight structure.

questions.q: The inspection guideline concerning WHO should inspect requires that inspectors:
o: Be independent from the authors with no conflict of interest
Report only to the project budget owner
Focus solely on cosmetic wording
Be the authors of the requirements document
questions.e: The WHO guideline states inspectors should be independent from the authors, have no conflict of interest or role evaluating them personally, and be representative of all stakeholders.

questions.q: In a defect-based requirements inspection checklist, the question "Is this concept precisely defined somewhere?" targets which defect type?
o: Noise
Contradiction
Ambiguity
Omission
questions.e: In the defect-based checklist, omission is checked by asking whether a concept is precisely defined somewhere; contradiction, inadequacy, ambiguity and noise are separate defect categories.

questions.q: In the defect-based checklist, the defect category identified by asking "Is this statement relevant to system objectives and constraints? Has this already been said without any reason for redundancy?" is:
o: Inadequacy
Ambiguity
Omission
Noise
questions.e: Noise is the checklist category concerned with whether a statement is relevant to system objectives and constraints and whether it has already been stated without any reason for redundancy.

questions.q: Which standard describes recommended approaches for the specification of software requirements and defines mandatory qualities for individual requirements?
o: IEEE 1012
ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
Fagan 1986
ISO 9001
questions.e: ISO/IEC/IEEE Standard 29148 describes recommended approaches for specifying software requirements and specifies qualities for individual requirements and for the set as a whole.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the mandatory qualities for an individual requirement under IEEE 29148?
o: Feasible
Bounded
Traceable
Singular
questions.e: The mandatory individual-requirement qualities are singular, feasible, unambiguous, complete, consistent, verifiable and traceable; 'bounded' is instead a characteristic of the collective SRS document.

questions.q: Regarding prototyping as a validation tool, which statement is true?
o: Prototypes reliably uncover all nonfunctional requirements
Prototypes replace the need for stakeholder shared understanding
Proof-of-concept prototypes can demonstrate that requirements are feasible
Prototypes are only useful after development and testing
questions.e: Proof-of-concept prototypes can demonstrate feasibility of requirements, but prototypes are not always effective at uncovering nonfunctional requirements, especially in novel systems.

questions.q: Why is simply designing test cases valuable for requirements validation, even before any tests are executed?
o: It removes the need for inspections
It guarantees the system will pass acceptance
It can reveal many problems with the requirements and expose vague or ambiguous statements
It automatically generates the source code
questions.e: Designing test cases can reveal many requirements problems long before execution; vague and ambiguous requirements stand out because they fail to define the expected system response.

questions.q: The 'Queries on Requirements Database' technique is characterised as:
o: A goal-refinement method
A tool-supported approach effective for large specifications using diagrammatic notations
A prototyping method for user interfaces
An informal manual review best for small documents
questions.e: Queries on the requirements database is a tool-supported approach effective for large specifications expressed in diagrammatic notations, enabling structural consistency and completeness checks.

questions.q: What distinguishes a requirements validation matrix from a requirements verification matrix?
o: The validation matrix associates high-level requirements with system attributes for trade-off analysis; the verification matrix associates requirements with test cases
The validation matrix associates requirements with test cases; the verification matrix with system attributes
Both associate requirements only with test cases
Both associate requirements only with business needs
questions.e: A requirements validation matrix associates high-level requirements with system attributes (e.g. business need, safety, volatility) for trade-off analysis, whereas the verification matrix associates requirements with the test cases that verify them.

questions.q: The concluding position on inspections and reviews states that inspection is:
o: Less effective than any other technique
Only applicable to source code
The most widely used and formalised approach to requirements validation
Rarely used and hard to formalise
questions.e: The conclusion states inspections and reviews can in principle detect any kind of defect in any specification format, and inspection is the most widely used and formalised approach to requirements validation.

questions.q: What is the alternative name given to requirements prioritization, as attributed to Davis (2005)?
o: Requirements velocity
Requirements triage
Requirements baselining
Requirements scrubbing
questions.e: Prioritization is also called requirements triage (Davis 2005); it helps reveal competing goals, resolve conflicts, plan for staged deliveries, control scope creep, and make trade-off decisions.

questions.q: According to the guiding principle for prioritization, the highest priority requirements are those that provide which of the following?
o: The features requested by the greatest number of stakeholders
The largest fraction of the total product value at the smallest fraction of the total cost
The largest fraction of the total cost regardless of value
The requirements that are easiest to implement technically
questions.e: The highest priority requirements are those that provide the largest fraction of the total product value at the smallest fraction of the total cost, delivering maximum value at minimum cost.

questions.q: In an Agile context, how do developers determine how many backlog stories they can fit into each iteration?
o: By estimating the effort per story and using the team's empirically demonstrated velocity
By having the project manager unilaterally assign stories
By implementing every story the customer marks as 'Must'
By using the $100 allocation to buy stories
questions.e: Developers estimate the effort of implementing each story and judge how many fit into each iteration based on their empirically demonstrated delivery capacity, measured by the team's velocity.

questions.q: A project manager must balance the desired project scope against which set of constraints?
o: Schedule, budget, staff, and quality goals
Velocity, backlog, and iterations
Importance, urgency, and politics
Value, cost, and risk only
questions.e: A project manager must balance desired project scope against the constraints of schedule, budget, staff, and quality goals; when more essential requirements are accepted, low priority ones can be dropped or deferred.

questions.q: What happens if customers do not distinguish their requirements by importance and urgency?
o: Project managers must make these prioritization decisions on their own
The project is automatically cancelled
All requirements are automatically classified as 'Must'
The requirements are all treated as low priority by default
questions.e: If customers don't distinguish their requirements by importance and urgency, project managers must make these decisions on their own; prioritization is a dynamic and ongoing process.

questions.q: Which prioritization technique is described as the simplest of all prioritization methods?
o: Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)
In or Out
$100 allocation
Pairwise comparison
questions.e: In or Out is the simplest of all prioritization methods: a group of stakeholders works down a list of requirements and makes a binary decision for each one about whether it is in or out for the release.

questions.q: In the 'In or Out' method, what kind of decision do stakeholders make about each requirement?
o: A ranking on a three-level scale
A pairwise comparison against every other requirement
A binary decision of whether it is in or out for this release
A dollar allocation from a fixed budget
questions.e: In the In or Out method, stakeholders make a binary decision for each requirement, paring the list down to the bare minimum needed for the first release; previously 'out' items can be reconsidered for the next release.

questions.q: Why does pairwise comparison and rank ordering become impractical for large sets of requirements?
o: It only works for requirements of different types
Performing the comparisons becomes very difficult for more than a couple of dozen requirements
It requires a fixed budget of 100 imaginary dollars
It can only be applied to defect stories
questions.e: Pairwise comparison judges which member of each pair has higher priority, but the comparisons become very difficult for more than a couple of dozen requirements; it works at the feature granularity, not for all functional requirements of a whole system.

questions.q: The common three-level prioritization scale groups requirements into which categories?
o: High, Medium, and Low priority
In, Out, and Deferred
Value, Cost, and Risk
Must, Should, and Could
questions.e: A common approach groups requirements into three categories: High, Medium, and Low priority. These scales are subjective, so stakeholders must agree on what each level means.

questions.q: In the three-level scale, priority is assessed along which two dimensions?
o: Value and cost
Risk and compliance
Effort and velocity
Importance and urgency
questions.e: One way to assess priority is to consider the two dimensions of importance (customers need the capability) and urgency (customers need it in the next release).

questions.q: In the three-level scale based on importance and urgency, a high-priority requirement is characterized as being:
o: Important but not urgent
Both important and urgent
Neither important nor urgent
Urgent but not important
questions.e: High-priority requirements are both important (customers need the capability) and urgent (customers need it in the next release), sometimes due to contractual, compliance, or compelling business reasons.

questions.q: How is a medium-priority requirement defined in the importance-and-urgency scale?
o: Important but not urgent, meaning it can wait for a later release
Both important and urgent
Urgent but not important
Neither important nor urgent
questions.e: Medium-priority requirements are important (customers need the capability) but not urgent (they can wait for a later release).

questions.q: In the importance-and-urgency scheme, requirements that appear urgent to some stakeholder (perhaps for political reasons) but are not important to the business objectives should be:
o: Set to low priority or scrubbed entirely
Automatically classified as high priority
Implemented first to satisfy the stakeholder
Rated as 'Should' under MoSCoW
questions.e: The fourth quadrant contains requirements that seem urgent to some stakeholder, perhaps for political reasons, but aren't important to the business objectives; because they don't add sufficient value, they should be set to low priority or scrubbed entirely.

questions.q: What do the four capitalized letters in the MoSCoW prioritization scheme stand for?
o: Mandatory, Standard, Common, and Wanted
Must, Should, Could, and Won't
Major, Significant, Cosmetic, and Withdrawn
Must, Should, Considered, and Waived
questions.e: The capitalized letters in MoSCoW stand for four priority classifications: Must (required for success), Should (important but not mandatory), Could (desirable but deferrable), and Won't (not implemented at this time).

questions.q: Under MoSCoW, how is a requirement rated 'Should' described?
o: A desirable capability that could be deferred or eliminated
Important and should be included if possible, but not mandatory to success
Will not be implemented now but could appear in a future release
Must be satisfied for the solution to be considered a success
questions.e: In MoSCoW, 'Should' means the requirement is important and should be included in the solution if possible, but it is not mandatory to success; this distinguishes it from the mandatory 'Must'.

questions.q: What is identified as a key source of ambiguity in the MoSCoW scheme?
o: The 'Must' rating has no defined meaning
The 'Won't' rating could mean either 'not in the next release' or 'not ever'
It requires allocating exactly 100 dollars
It only allows three priority levels
questions.e: MoSCoW is ambiguous as to timing, particularly with 'Won't,' which could mean either 'not in the next release' or 'not ever'; such distinctions must be made clear so stakeholders share a common understanding.

questions.q: How does the MoSCoW scheme relate to the three-level high/medium/low scale?
o: It merges the three levels into a single binary in/out decision
It adds dollar values to each of the three levels
It changes the three-level scale into a four-level scale without offering any rationale
It removes the concept of urgency from the three levels
questions.e: MoSCoW changes the three-level scale of high, medium, and low into a four-level scale without offering any rationale; it is described as ambiguous and is not a recommended approach compared with the crisper importance/urgency analysis.

questions.q: In the $100 method, if one requirement is three times as important to a stakeholder as another, how might the stakeholder allocate the imaginary dollars?
o: Nine dollars to the first requirement and three dollars to the second
Fifty dollars to each requirement
One hundred dollars to the first and zero to the second
Three dollars to the first and nine dollars to the second
questions.e: In the $100 method, higher-priority requirements are weighted more heavily; if one requirement is three times as important as another, a stakeholder might assign nine dollars to the first and three dollars to the second, drawing from a fixed pool of 100 imaginary dollars.

questions.q: What fundamental constraint governs how team members allocate money in the $100 prioritization method?
o: Each requirement must receive an equal share of the dollars
Only 100 dollars are available, so when the money runs out nothing else can be implemented in the current release
Dollars can be borrowed from future releases if needed
Only 'Must' requirements are eligible to receive dollars
questions.e: The prioritization team is given 100 imaginary dollars to buy candidate requirements; 100 dollars is all they get, so when they are out of money nothing else can be implemented, at least not in the release they are currently focusing on.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the other formal and complex prioritization approaches that can be used?
o: Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)
In or Out
Three-level scale
MoSCoW scale
questions.e: Other formal and complex approaches that can be used include QFD, the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), and Value, Cost & Risk analysis, in addition to the simpler techniques.

questions.q: What guidance is given about the complexity of the prioritization process itself?
o: Always use the most formal and complex technique available
Let a single technique such as MoSCoW handle every situation
Keep the prioritization process as simple as possible, but no simpler
Prioritize only once at the end of the project
questions.e: The recommended guidance is to keep the prioritization process as simple as possible, but no simpler, and to move prioritization away from the political and emotional arena so stakeholders can make honest assessments.

questions.q: When choosing a level of abstraction for prioritization amid too many requirement types, what is recommended regarding decision-making authority among the various stakeholders?
o: Avoid involving customers or project sponsors
Prioritize only individual functional requirements, never features
Let every stakeholder have equal veto power
Decide on one ultimate decision maker
questions.e: Because various stakeholders (customers, sponsors, project management, development, and others) participate in prioritization, it is recommended to decide on one ultimate decision maker, while choosing an appropriate abstraction level such as features or user stories.

questions.q: How does the recommended approach differ between smaller and larger projects?
o: Informal consensus can work for smaller projects, while large projects require formal and structured approaches
Smaller projects require formal approaches, while large projects use informal consensus
Neither type of project should prioritize requirements
Both require the $100 method exclusively
questions.e: For smaller projects, informal consensus can work, but large projects require formal and structured approaches to prioritization.
